course_158_la_tragedie_grecque_et_le_the.explanation: A group of 12 to 15 citizens who sing, dance, and comment on the action between episodes. The chorus represents the voice of the community and provides a moral perspective on the heroes' actions. Its role gradually diminished under Sophocles and Euripides.

An ancient theater from the 4th century BC, capable of seating 14,000 spectators. Its extraordinary acoustics (a coin drop can be heard from any seat) remain mysterious and surpass the capabilities of modern acoustic engineering.

course_159_le_theatre_de_shakespeare|159.explanation: A theater built on the south bank of the Thames, outside the limits of the City of London (which banned performances). Octagonal and open to the sky, it hosted 3,000 spectators standing (the "groundlings") or seated in the covered galleries.

course_159_le_theatre_de_shakespeare|gro.explanation: The least wealthy spectators of Elizabethan theater who, for a penny, attended the performance standing in the open-air pit.

course_160_la_liberte_de_la_presse_et_le.explanation: Fundamental tension: how far should a photographer get involved? Kevin Carter photographed a vulture waiting for a Sudanese child to die (1993) and was accused of not helping. He received the Pulitzer then committed suicide three months later.

course_162_promethee_le_voleur_de_feu|Pr.explanation: Prometheus has become the symbol of human emancipation through knowledge, defying the limits set by the gods. Goethe, Shelley (Frankenstein), Marx claimed him as a symbol - he embodies the modernity rebelling against the established order.

course_162_promethee_le_voleur_de_feu|br.explanation: His name means "the one who thinks after". He accepted without thinking Pandora's gift sent by Zeus. His recklessness introduced evils into the world. The Prometheus-Epimetheus pair illustrates the opposition between foresight and impulsivity.

course_163_pandore_et_la_boite|Hope.explanation: In Hesiod's version, Hope remains in the jar when Pandora closes it. A fundamental ambiguity: is it the last benevolent gift from the gods, or an additional evil (false hope, illusion) that tortures men by making them believe things will improve?

course_163_pandore_et_la_boite|Elpis.explanation: In Hesiod's version, Hope remains in the jar when Pandora closes it. A fundamental ambiguity: is it the last benevolent gift from the gods, or an additional evil (false hope, illusion) that tortures men by making them believe things will improve?

course_163_pandore_et_la_boite|misogyny.explanation: Contempt or hostility toward women, illustrated in this myth by the creation of Pandora as a punishment.

course_164_demeter_et_persephone_les_sai.explanation: Secret initiation ceremonies celebrated at Eleusis for over a millennium (600 BC - 400 AD). Based on the myth of Persephone, they promised initiates a blissful life after death. Plato and Marcus Aurelius were initiated into them.

The myth of Persephone is a mythological explanation of the vegetative cycle: when she descends into the Underworld (autumn-winter), the earth is sterile; when she ascends (spring), the vegetation is reborn. Greek religion was linked to agricultural rhythms.

course_165_orphee_et_eurydice|catabasis.explanation: The descent into the Underworld. A recurring mythological motif: the hero descends into the Underworld alive (Heracles, Odysseus, Aeneas, Orpheus). This journey symbolizes initiation through death and confrontation with the unconscious.

course_166_narcisse_et_echo|echo in acou.explanation: The repercussion of a sound on a surface and its return to its source. The word "echo" comes directly from the nymph in the myth, condemned to only repeat the last words heard. This myth explained the natural acoustic phenomenon to the Greeks.

course_166_narcisse_et_echo|psychology.explanation: Term coined by Freud in 1914: excessive love of oneself, and an inability to love anyone else. In the myth, Narcissus cannot love Echo because he loves only his own image. Freud separated healthy early narcissism from the harmful kind.

course_166_narcisse_et_echo|Narcissism.explanation: Term coined by Freud in 1914: excessive love of oneself, and an inability to love anyone else. In the myth, Narcissus cannot love Echo because he loves only his own image. Freud separated healthy early narcissism from the harmful kind.

course_166_narcisse_et_echo|acoustic phy.explanation: The repercussion of a sound against a surface and its return to its source. The word "echo" comes directly from the nymph of the myth, condemned to only repeat the last words heard. This myth explained the natural acoustic phenomenon to the Greeks.

course_166_narcisse_et_echo|Echo.explanation: The repercussion of a sound against a surface and its return to its source. The word "echo" comes directly from the nymph of the myth, condemned to only repeat the last words heard. This myth explained the natural acoustic phenomenon to the Greeks.

course_167_icare_et_dedale|labyrinth as.explanation: Daedalus's construction imprisoning the Minotaur. Beyond the myth, the Labyrinth has become a universal symbol of wandering, of the quest and the impossible return - of the unconscious or of inextricable destiny.

course_167_icare_et_dedale|and excess.explanation: Icarus embodies classic hubris: refusing to respect human limits and trying to rise to the level of the gods. Greek myth always punishes that transgression, because the Greeks saw excess as the worst of all tragic faults.

course_167_icare_et_dedale|Hybris.explanation: Icarus embodies classic hubris: refusing to respect human limits and trying to rise to the level of the gods. Greek myth always punishes that transgression, because the Greeks saw excess as the worst of all tragic faults.

course_167_icare_et_dedale|metis.explanation: Form of Greek intelligence characterized by cunning, technical skill and the ability to adapt to complex situations. It is the hallmark of Daedalus and Odysseus.

course_168_sisyphe_punition_eternelle|ab.explanation: In The Myth of Sisyphus (1942), Camus chooses this myth because Sisyphus knows his fate and continues anyway. Camus concludes that "one must imagine Sisyphus happy" - only the refusal of resignation makes the absurd bearable.

course_168_sisyphe_punition_eternelle|hu.explanation: Sisyphus was punished for having cheated death twice and revealed secrets of the gods. In Greek mythology, mortals who defied the divine order or claimed immortality received eternal and exemplary punishments.

course_169_tantale_et_son_supplice|\"tan.explanation: Expression describing any situation where what one desires is almost within reach but always inaccessible. This universal symbol of frustration and temptation has crossed all cultures and is found in psychological theories on desire.

course_169_tantale_et_son_supplice|Ta, 7.explanation: Named as such in 1802 by Ekeberg because it is insoluble in acids - like Tantalus who can swallow nothing. It is used in capacitors for smartphones and in biocompatible medical prostheses.

course_170_meduse_et_persee|Gorgoneion.explanation: Representation of the head of Medusa used as an Apotropaic amulet (to ward off evil) throughout ancient Greece. It was found on temples, shields, rings, mosaics. It passed into Roman art and then into medieval coats of arms.

course_170_meduse_et_persee|birth of.explanation: When Perseus beheads Medusa, the winged horse Pegasus is born from her blood. Bellerophon later captures him with Athena's help and rides him to defeat the Chimera. Pegasus has become the universal symbol of poetic inspiration.

course_170_meduse_et_persee|Pegasus.explanation: When Perseus beheads Medusa, the winged horse Pegasus is born from her blood. Bellerophon later captures him with Athena's help and rides him to defeat the Chimera. Pegasus has become the universal symbol of poetic inspiration.

course_170_meduse_et_persee|harpe.explanation: Type of saber or sickle with a curved blade used by Perseus to slice through Medusa's scaly neck.

course_171_hercule_et_ses_12_travaux|Pil.explanation: The headlands at Gibraltar that ancient tradition treated as the edge of the known world. The phrase "nec plus ultra" was attached to them. Columbus sailed past them in 1492 and pushed the edge of the known world westward.

course_171_hercule_et_ses_12_travaux|leo.explanation: Skin of the Nemean lion worn by Heracles as armor. It is his main attribute in iconography.

course_171_hercule_et_ses_12_travaux|cen.explanation: Mythological creature half-man, half-horse. The blood of the centaur Nessus will cause the physical death of Heracles.

course_172_thesee_et_le_minotaure|Labyri.explanation: Excavations at Knossos revealed the Minoan palace, with its complex layout evoking a labyrinth. The Minoan civilization (2700-1450 BC) and its bull cult are likely at the origin of the myth of the Minotaur.

course_173_ulysse_et_le_cyclope|cunning.explanation: Practical intelligence, cunning, the ability to turn a bad situation around. Odysseus is its perfect example, and his Homeric epithet is "of many wiles". It stands opposed to biē, the brute force embodied by Ajax.

course_173_ulysse_et_le_cyclope|Metis i.explanation: Practical intelligence, cunning, the ability to turn a bad situation around. Odysseus is its perfect example, and his Homeric epithet is "of many wiles". It stands opposed to biē, the brute force embodied by Ajax.

course_173_ulysse_et_le_cyclope|Cyclopes.explanation: One-eyed beings, sons of Uranus and Gaia: divine blacksmiths who forged the lightning of Zeus. In Homer, Polyphemus and his kind are wild shepherds ignorant of the gods and laws - an embodiment of barbarism.

course_175_jason_et_la_toison_d_or|moder.explanation: Region east of the Black Sea, described in Greek myths as the end of the eastern world. Shepherds there used sheep fleeces to filter gold from the gold-bearing rivers of the Caucasus - the "golden fleece" may have been real.

course_176_achille_le_talon_et_l_invulne.explanation: Supreme value of heroic culture: immortal glory acquired through warlike exploits and transmitted by poets. Achilles deliberately chooses a short but glorious life over a long life without glory - a fundamental choice of Greek heroic ethics.

Achilles' elite warriors, legendarily created by Zeus from ants (myrmex = ant in Greek). In the Iliad, they are the most feared soldiers. Their absolute loyalty to Achilles illustrates the unbreakable bond between a hero and his men.
The highlight of an epic tale where a hero shines through their warrior exploits and absolute superiority on the battlefield.
Greek notion designating the excess of pride or the hubris of a human who believes themselves to be the equal of the gods and ends up being punished.

course_177_dipe_et_le_sphinx|Sphinx in w.explanation: Hybrid creature present in many cultures: Egyptian Sphinx (lion, human head, royal symbol) and Greek Sphinx (female, winged, poser of deadly riddles). The same image takes on opposite meanings depending on the culture.

course_178_antigone_devoir_familial_vs_l.explanation: Hegel was the first, in 1807, to argue that in Antigone both characters are right by their own principle: family against state, divine law against human law. This is not good against evil but two goods that cannot both be honored, which is the very definition of the tragic.

Play performed in Paris under the Nazi occupation. Anouilh deliberately left its political meaning open: Creon could stand for the Germans or for Vichy, Antigone for the Resistance. Both sides found what they wanted in it, which was either genius or opportunism.

course_180_thor_et_loki_mythologie_nordi.explanation: A 13th-century Icelandic treatise on poetry and myth. Although it was written by a Christian, it is the most organized source we have on Norse belief, and it was meant to preserve the craft of the old poets.

course_182_osiris_et_set_mythologie_egyp.explanation: Fundamental principle of Egyptian thought: cosmic order, truth and justice. The pharaoh was responsible for maintaining Ma'at against chaos. Osiris presides over the judgment of the dead, weighing their heart against the feather of Ma'at.

A collection of magical spells accompanying deceased Egyptians into the afterlife. It guided the soul through the trials of the underworld, notably the judgment before Osiris. Some illustrated papyri are among the most beautiful works of Egyptian art.

course_183_gilgamesh_le_premier_heros_de.explanation: A collective term for the civilizations of the Fertile Crescent between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers (modern Iraq). They invented cuneiform writing, codified law (Code of Hammurabi), sexagesimal mathematics and astronomy.

Tablet XI of the Epic contains a universal Flood myth earlier than the biblical Deluge: Utnapishtim builds a boat and brings all the animals on board. This parallel stunned biblical scholars when it was discovered in 1872.

course_184_romulus_et_remus_la_fondation.explanation: The traditional Date of the founding of Rome, calculated by Varro in the 1st century BC. The Romans counted years "from the founding of the city" (AUC). This legendary Date corresponded to the monarchy of the seven kings of Rome.

A bronze statue of a she-wolf suckling Romulus and Remus, symbol of Rome. Long believed to be Etrusque (5th century BC), recent studies date it to the Middle Ages. The human twins were added by Pollaiolo in the 15th century.

course_185_vishnou_et_shiva_mythologie_h.explanation: Central philosophical text of Hinduism extracted from the Mahabharata: Krishna (avatar of Vishnu) explains to Arjuna the meaning of duty (dharma) and selfless action before the battle. Admired by Thoreau, Emerson, Gandhi, and Oppenheimer.
Small hourglass-shaped drum held by Shiva, whose sound symbolizes the rhythm of the original creation.

course_186_les_valkyries_et_le_valhalla|.explanation: Richard Wagner set Norse mythology to music in Der Ring des Nibelungen (1848-1874). "The Ride of the Valkyries" is among the best-known works of classical music in the world, often associated with American cinema.

course_187_le_phenix_a_travers_les_cultu.explanation: The Phoenix bird was adopted by alchemists as a symbol of transmutation: as it is reborn from its ashes, base metals can be transformed into gold. Its presence is recurrent in hermetic and esoteric literature.

Chinese mythological bird symbol of virtue and grace, associated with the Empress (as the dragon is with the Emperor). Its reappearance announced a virtuous and just reign. It embodies the five Confucian virtues.

course_188_les_titans_vs_les_dieux_titan.explanation: After the Titanomachy, the Olympians had to face the giants (born from the blood of Uranus), who were nearly invincible. This second war of the gods foreshadows the permanent tensions between Olympian order and the primordial forces of chaos.

course_189_dionysos_le_dieu_du_vin_et_de.explanation: Greek tragedies and comedies were born from Dionysian rituals. Thespis (6th century) was the first to introduce an actor distinct from the chorus - the founding act of Western theater. The theater of Athens was itself a place of worship for Dionysus.
Philosophical opposition between order/reason (Apollo) and chaos/intoxication (Dionysos) as drivers of artistic creation.

Secret and initiatory religious rites guaranteeing the faithful a direct experience of the divine or a favorable fate in the afterlife.
Aristotelian term designating the purgation or purification of passions (pity and fear) in the spectator of a tragedy.

course_191_enee_et_la_fondation_de_rome_.explanation: Major poem by Dante Alighieri (14th century) where Virgil appears as the narrator's guide through Hell and Purgatory.
Legendary conflict pitting the Greek states against the Trojans, serving as the chronological starting point for the Aeneid.

The classical verse form of Greek and Latin epic poetry, composed of six rhythmic units (feet).
A term meaning 'proppings,' referring to the verses that Virgil left unfinished in his manuscript while waiting to find a perfect formulation.

Fundamental virtue according to Virgil: devotion to the gods, the homeland, and the family. Aeneas is the "pious Aeneas" - he escapes from Troy carrying his old father on his back. This value embodies the Roman ideal in opposition to Greek hybris.

course_192_les_dieux_azteques_et_les_sac.displayTerm: cosmology of the Five Suns and the cosmic debt
course_192_les_dieux_azteques_et_les_sac.explanation: The gods had sacrificed their blood to create the fifth sun. Humans were in perpetual debt and had to repay with blood. This logic of cosmic exchange made sacrifices morally necessary in the Aztec vision of the world.
God of the Sun and war, protector of the Mexica. As the sun must "fight" darkness every morning, he needs the blood of captured warriors to complete his daily journey and rise again.

course_194_le_mahabharata|Bhagavad Gita.displayTerm: Bhagavad Gita as a philosophical text
course_194_le_mahabharata|Bhagavad Gita.explanation: The 18 chapters of dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna constitute a major philosophical text, independent of the rest of the epic. Krishna teaches selfless action (karma yoga), devotion (bhakti) and knowledge (jnana) as paths to liberation.

course_194_le_mahabharata|Orality and tr.displayTerm: Orality and transmission of Indian epics
course_194_le_mahabharata|Orality and tr.explanation: Like Homer, The Mahabharata was originally an oral epic memorized and recited by griots. Its transcription stretched over several centuries. These texts are still recited and sung throughout India, as alive as ever.

course_194_le_mahabharata|Bhagavad-Gita.explanation: The 18 chapters of dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna constitute a major philosophical text, independent of the rest of the epic. Krishna teaches selfless action (Karma yoga), devotion (bhakti), and knowledge (jnana) as paths to liberation.

course_195_lancelot_guenievre_et_la_tabl.explanation: Social code glorifying the secret and inaccessible love of a knight for a lady (often married). Lancelot and Guinevere are the perfect example. This adulterous passion, destructive yet sublime, is at the heart of medieval Literature.

A situation where water demand exceeds available resources or when water quality limits its use. We speak of severe scarcity below the threshold of 1,000 m³ per inhabitant/year.

course_236_le_soft_power_americain|Grams.explanation: Concept by theorist Antonio Gramsci: a dominant class maintains its power by making its values accepted as natural and universal. Joseph Nye adapted this idea to international relations with the concept of soft power.

course_236_le_soft_power_americain|\"Bru.explanation: European regulatory standards (GDPR, food standards, environmental standards) are adopted globally by multinationals wishing to access the market of 450 million consumers. The EU thus exercises considerable regulatory soft power.

course_237_les_gafam_puissance_et_derive.explanation: European law aiming to regulate the "gatekeepers" of digital markets. It mandates interoperability and prohibits favoritism of its own services. It is the most ambitious regulation of GAFAM in the world.

course_239_le_futur_du_travail|Schumpete.explanation: Each innovation destroys obsolete jobs and creates new ones. History seems to prove Schumpeter right (from the farmer to the driver). The question is whether AI, which also affects skilled jobs, will reproduce this pattern or break it for good.

course_239_le_futur_du_travail|Creative.explanation: Each innovation destroys obsolete jobs and creates new ones. History seems to prove Schumpeter right (from the farmer to the driver). The question is whether AI, which also affects skilled jobs, will reproduce this pattern or break it for good.

course_239_le_futur_du_travail|32 hours.explanation: Reduction of the work week while maintaining salary. Experiments in Iceland, Japan, Spain, and Great Britain show positive results: productivity maintained or improved, increased well-being, reduced absenteeism.

course_239_le_futur_du_travail|The 4-day.explanation: Reduction of the work week while maintaining salary. Experiments in Iceland, Japan, Spain, and Great Britain show positive results: productivity maintained or improved, increased well-being, reduced absenteeism.

course_240_la_chine_et_son_modele_econom.explanation: Single party in power since 1949, with 98 million members. It controls the state, the army, the media, and increasingly the economy. The General Secretary (Xi Jinping since 2012) is the true leader of the country.

course_241_pourquoi_voulait_on_demolir_l.explanation: A vast open space in Paris between the École Militaire and the Seine, where several Universal Exhibitions were held. The Eiffel Tower stands at its river end.
A great international fair held in Paris from May to October 1889 for the centenary of the French Revolution. Every country showed its inventions, products and arts. The Eiffel Tower was its gateway.
French engineer and entrepreneur (1832-1923), a specialist in metal structures: bridges, stations, viaducts. His firm built the tower that bears his name and the framework of the Statue of Liberty.

An open letter published in Le Temps on February 14, 1887, signed by about fifty writers, painters and architects, including Maupassant, Gounod and Garnier. It denounced the tower as "useless and monstrous."

In the nineteenth century, the wealthy urban class: industrialists, bankers, notables. It set the tone of official taste in art and architecture, attached to styles inherited from antiquity and the Renaissance.
The ancestor of radio: sending Morse-code messages by electromagnetic waves, without a cable. The Eiffel Tower served as an antenna from 1903 and became a military listening post.

course_242_pourquoi_a_t_on_le_hoquet|ref.explanation: A short neural circuit that triggers an automatic response to a stimulus, without any conscious decision. The signal travels to the spinal cord or brainstem, which immediately sends an order back to the muscles.

course_242_pourquoi_a_t_on_le_hoquet|dia.explanation: A large dome-shaped muscle below the lungs. When it contracts, it flattens and draws air in: it is the main muscle of breathing.

course_242_pourquoi_a_t_on_le_hoquet|glo.explanation: The opening between the vocal cords at the top of the windpipe. It closes to protect the airways and opens to let air through.

course_242_pourquoi_a_t_on_le_hoquet|int.explanation: Hiccups that last more than a month. Very rare, they almost always point to an underlying disease and call for medical care.

course_242_pourquoi_a_t_on_le_hoquet|Cha.explanation: An Iowa farmer (1894-1991) who entered Guinness World Records for the longest known attack of hiccups: 68 years, from 1922 to 1990.

course_243_pourquoi_a_t_on_invente_les_v.explanation: Greek scholar (1586-1669) and Vatican librarian. In a 1645 treatise on Greek popular beliefs, he described the vrykolakas, a dead man who returns to torment the living.
In Greek folklore, a corpse that refuses to decay and goes out at night to knock on doors and torment the living, often its own relatives. Only fire can destroy it.

A Serbian peasant from the village of Kisiljevo who died in 1725. Accused by his dying neighbors of coming back to smother them, he was exhumed and staked in front of an Austrian official, whose report spread the word "vampire" across Europe.
An infectious lung disease caused by a bacterium, highly contagious and long fatal. Known as "consumption," it made its victims waste away, cough and grow pale for months.
A 19-year-old woman who died of tuberculosis in Exeter, Rhode Island, in 1892. Her exhumation by neighbors convinced she was draining her brother's strength is the last great American "vampire case."
English doctor and writer (1795-1821), traveling companion of Lord Byron. His story The Vampyre (1819) invented the aristocratic, seductive vampire.
Irish writer (1847-1912) and theater manager in London. His novel Dracula (1897) fixed the modern image of the vampire.

course_149_la_joconde|Francis I.explanation: King of France and patron of the arts who welcomed Leonardo da Vinci to Amboise. The Mona Lisa entered his collection after Leonardo carried it to France in 1517, long before it reached the Louvre.

course_149_la_joconde|Giorgio Vasari.explanation: Sixteenth-century Italian painter, architect and writer, author of the Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects, published in 1550 and 1568. His biography of Leonardo is the source that names the sitter of the Mona Lisa, though historians see part of it as literary invention.

course_149_la_joconde|Battle of Anghiari.explanation: Large mural commissioned from Leonardo in October 1503 by the Florentine Republic to commemorate its victory over Milan in 1440. Left unfinished and known only through sketches and copies, it drew Leonardo away from the portrait of Lisa Gherardini.

course_149_la_joconde|Palazzo Vecchio.explanation: Fortified palace in the center of Florence, seat of the government of the Florentine Republic. Leonardo was to paint the Battle of Anghiari in one of its halls, a public commission held to be far more prestigious than a private portrait.

course_149_la_joconde|varnish.explanation: Transparent coat applied over an oil painting to protect it, which yellows with age. The Mona Lisa's varnish has not been removed in modern times, for fear of damaging the work and of breaking the icon's spell.

course_214_la_crise_de_l_etat_providence.explanation: The set of protections a state funds through taxes and contributions: pensions, medical care, unemployment and family benefits. The course shows that, from the postwar years on, France and the United States reserved its full rights for their citizens.

The highest court in the French judicial system, housed in the Palais de Justice in Paris. It does not retry the facts but checks how the law was applied; in 1991 it struck down the pension refusal opposed to Mazari on grounds of nationality.

An American program that recruited Mexican farmworkers on temporary contracts requiring their return to Mexico. From July 1951, these workers were excluded from Social Security, even as their employers profited from their labor.

The historian Mae Ngai's term for bringing foreign workers into a country's economy without a secure place in its political community or access to its social rights. It describes the fate of Mexican braceros in the United States.

A French philosopher known for his work on citizenship, the nation and the borders of Europe. The course draws on his analysis of the idea of a "threshold of tolerance" and its political uses against immigrants.

The idea that a society can absorb only a limited proportion of immigrants before living together becomes impossible. Étienne Balibar shows that it serves, on the right and on the left, to blame immigrants for unemployment, housing shortages and overcrowded hospitals.

Leader of the French Communist Party, of which he was general secretary for more than twenty years. In 1980 he defended the mayor of Vitry-sur-Seine after a bulldozer was sent against a hostel of Malian workers, citing the town's limited capacity to take in more immigrants.

course_234_la_securite_alimentaire_mondi.explanation: The condition of a person whose diet is insufficient or unbalanced, in quantity or in quality. It affects 7% of children under five, even though the planet grows enough food for everyone.
The series of steps that carry food from field to plate: harvest, processing, transport, storage, sale. The longer it stretches with globalization, the more weak links it has where food gets lost.

Everything a farmer brings in from outside in order to produce: fertilizer, pesticides, water, energy, seeds, labor. Producing more with fewer inputs is the key to more efficient and more sustainable farming.

Food fit to eat that ends up thrown away, at the retailer, in restaurants or at home. Together with losses earlier in the chain, it amounts to a third of world production, some 1.3 billion tons a year.

The knitting together of the world's economies through trade, here the trade in farm products between continents. It allows imports all year round, but lengthens supply chains and makes them more vulnerable.

A method that measures the state of soil and crops in real time, with sensors, robots or drones, in order to apply only the dose each patch needs. It lowers costs and environmental impact while optimizing yields.

course_244_d_ou_vient_le_loup_garou|Hero.explanation: Greek historian of the 5th century BC, often called the "father of history," author of a vast inquiry into the peoples and wars of his time. He reports that the Neuri turned into wolves, while making clear he does not believe it.

course_244_d_ou_vient_le_loup_garou|Neur.explanation: An ancient people living north of the Black Sea, known mainly through Herodotus. According to what he was told, each of them became a wolf for a few days every year: one of the earliest surviving accounts of a werewolf.

course_244_d_ou_vient_le_loup_garou|Lyca.explanation: Mythical king of Arcadia who serves human flesh to Jupiter to test whether he is really a god. Turned into a wolf as punishment, he is the oldest werewolf: a man whose body takes the shape of his cruelty.

course_244_d_ou_vient_le_loup_garou|Arca.explanation: A mountainous region in the central Peloponnese, in Greece, long seen as a land of shepherds cut off from the world. Ancient writers set the kingdom of Lycaon there, along with several tales of men turned into wolves.

course_244_d_ou_vient_le_loup_garou|Plin.explanation: Roman naturalist and writer of the 1st century, author of the huge Natural History, which gathers the knowledge of his time. In it he reports the case of Demaenetus, said to have lived for years as a wolf before becoming a man again.

course_244_d_ou_vient_le_loup_garou|Mari.explanation: A poet writing in French in the 12th century, probably at the English court, known for her short verse tales called lais. Her Bisclavret tells the story of a werewolf nobleman betrayed by his wife.

course_244_d_ou_vient_le_loup_garou|Bisc.explanation: A short verse tale by Marie de France, written in the 12th century, whose hero is a nobleman who regularly turns into a wolf. Robbed of his clothes by his wife, he stays a wolf but keeps his reason and his honor.

course_245_d_ou_vient_le_pere_noel|Nicho.explanation: Bishop of Myra, in Asia Minor (now Turkey), born around 270 and famous for giving his wealth to the poor. As Saint Nicholas, protector of children and sailors, he is the first piece of the Santa Claus legend.

course_245_d_ou_vient_le_pere_noel|patro.explanation: In Christian tradition, a saint regarded as the special protector of a group, a trade, a town or a country. Saint Nicholas is the patron of children and sailors, which explains his place in the midwinter holidays.

course_245_d_ou_vient_le_pere_noel|Sinte.explanation: The Dutch version of Saint Nicholas: a bishop in red miter and cope who rides through the towns on a white horse, staff in hand. Carried to America, his name slowly turned into Santa Claus.

course_245_d_ou_vient_le_pere_noel|Fathe.explanation: An English figure recorded since at least the 15th century: a jolly visitor clad in fur who personifies the feasting and celebration of midwinter. Originally, he brought no gifts to children.

course_245_d_ou_vient_le_pere_noel|Cleme.explanation: New York professor and writer (1779-1863) credited with the poem A Visit from St. Nicholas, published anonymously in 1823. The attribution, which he claimed in his lifetime, is still debated by scholars.

course_245_d_ou_vient_le_pere_noel|Thoma.explanation: German-born American cartoonist (1840-1902), famous for his political cartoons in Harper's Weekly. From 1863, he gave Santa Claus his round belly, his white beard and his North Pole workshop.

course_245_d_ou_vient_le_pere_noel|Haddo.explanation: American illustrator (1899-1976) who painted Coca-Cola's Christmas advertisements for more than thirty years, starting in 1931. His warm, grandfatherly Santa fixed the image the whole world recognizes today.

course_246_qui_etait_le_vrai_roi_arthur|.explanation: A Germanic people from the continent who settled in Britain from the 5th century, alongside the Angles and the Jutes. Their advance against the Britons forms the backdrop of the earliest stories about Arthur.
A British cleric of the 6th century, author of a sermon on the ruin of Britain describing the wars against the Saxons. It is the earliest source on the Battle of Badon, and it never names Arthur.

A major victory of the Britons over the Saxons, placed around 500, whose exact date and location remain disputed. Recorded by Gildas without a leader's name, it later became the defining triumph of Arthurian legend.

A Romano-British war leader of the 5th century, whom Gildas presents as the survivor of a prominent family destroyed by the Saxons and the first to rally the Britons. Later writers linked him to Arthur without any early evidence.

A Welsh writer traditionally credited with the Historia Brittonum, a Latin compilation of the 9th century. This text is the first to name Arthur, not as a king but as a "leader of battles" who defeated the Saxons.

A Welsh cleric of the 12th century, author of a History of the Kings of Britain that made Arthur a crowned, conquering and glorious king. Written after the Norman Conquest, his account founded the medieval Arthurian legend.

The seizure of England by William, Duke of Normandy, in 1066, which installed a new aristocracy from the continent. Its rulers sought an ancient legitimacy, which Geoffrey of Monmouth's Arthur came to provide.

course_247_pourquoi_les_momies_font_elle.explanation: The set of techniques that stop a body from decaying: drying, removal of the organs, resins, wrappings. In Egypt it served to guarantee the dead person an existence in the afterlife, not to frighten the living.

The period of Egyptian history running from about 1550 to 1070 BC, that of famous pharaohs such as Tutankhamun. It was the golden age of embalming, whose most elaborate form was reserved for the wealthiest.

A natural salt gathered from dried-up lakes in Egypt, a mixture of sodium carbonate and bicarbonate. Embalmers covered the body with it to draw out the water before rubbing it with oils and wrapping it in linen.

Powdered mummy sold as a remedy by European apothecaries from the Middle Ages to the early modern period. The name comes from mumiya, an Arabic word for a bituminous substance that markets confused with the embalmed bodies of Egypt.

British archaeologist (1874-1939) who discovered the almost intact tomb of Tutankhamun in the Valley of the Kings in 1922. His find made headlines around the world and fixed the legend of the mummy's curse.
A pharaoh of the New Kingdom who died very young in the 14th century BC. His reign was brief, but his almost intact tomb, discovered in 1922, made him the most famous of all pharaohs.
British aristocrat who financed Howard Carter's excavations in the Valley of the Kings. His death in 1923, after an illness, was immediately linked by the newspapers to a supposed curse of the tomb.

British actor (1887-1969) and star of Hollywood horror films after playing Frankenstein's monster in 1931. In The Mummy (1932), he gave the embalmed corpse a body that moves, chases and takes revenge.

course_248_pourquoi_les_sorcieres_volent.explanation: Dominican theologian of the early 13th century, one of the first masters of his order to teach in Paris. He recorded tales of night journeys and magical ointments, long before the broom entered the imagery of witches.

In the imagination of the witch trials, a nighttime assembly where witches gathered around the devil. To explain how accused women from distant villages could meet there, 15th-century judges imagined that they flew.
Salves that, according to early modern writers, witches rubbed on before their night journeys. Made from plants like nightshade and henbane, they could cause hallucinations and a sensation of flying.

A long poem by Martin Le Franc, written around 1440 in defense of women. In the margin of one of its manuscripts, two women labeled "Vaudoises" fly on a broom and on a staff: the earliest known image of witches in flight.

Augustinian prior and doctor of theology near Paris, at first skeptical of warnings against witchcraft. Arrested in 1453, he confessed under pressure to flying to the sabbath on a broom, repented and ended his life in prison.

The European intellectual movement of the 18th century that made observation, reason and evidence the judge of every claim. It made magical flight implausible, discredited confessions under torture and helped bring the witch trials to an end.

course_249_les_vikings_ont_ils_decouvert.explanation: Genoese navigator in the service of Spain who crossed the Atlantic in 1492 while looking for a route to Asia. His voyage opened a regular link between Europe and the Americas, something the Vikings never established.
Huge island in the North Atlantic, settled by the Norse after Iceland. It was from there that the expeditions to Vinland set out, in search of timber and new land.
Large island off the east coast of Canada. The Vinland of the sagas seems to have included part of it, and its northern tip is home to the Viking site of L'Anse aux Meadows.

The name given to two medieval Icelandic stories, the Saga of Erik the Red and the Saga of the Greenlanders, written in the 13th and 14th centuries. They tell of the Norse voyages to Helluland, Markland and Vinland.
Norse navigator from Greenland who, according to the sagas, reached Vinland around the year 1000. He is regarded as the first known European to have landed in North America.
Archaeological site on the northern tip of Newfoundland, discovered in the 1960s by Helge and Anne Stine Ingstad. Its eight Norse buildings prove that the Vikings did reach North America.

The name the sagas give to the peoples the Norse met in Vinland. It probably refers to Indigenous groups of North America, but the details of these contacts remain uncertain and their archaeological traces are thin.

course_250_comment_gengis_khan_a_t_il_co.explanation: Birth name of Genghis Khan, born in the 12th century on the Mongolian steppe. Fatherless at nine and abandoned by his clan, he united the Mongol tribes and founded the Mongol Empire before his death in 1227.
Vast treeless grassland with a harsh climate, stretching across Central Asia. It is the world of the nomadic herders and Mongol horsemen whom Temüjin turned into an army.

Empire founded by Genghis Khan in the early 13th century and expanded by his successors until it became the largest land empire in history. At its height it covered much of Eurasia and ruled over around 110 million people.
A policy that lets each community practice its own faith without coercion. For the Mongols it served as a tool of government: subjects free to pray to their own god had fewer reasons to rebel.

Relay network created by Genghis Khan, where the empire's messengers rested and changed horses. It carried orders and reports between the capital and the provinces, sometimes covering more than 200 miles in a day.
The single landmass formed by Europe and Asia together. The Mongol Empire stretched across much of it, from China in the east to the gates of Europe in the west.

course_251_pourquoi_londres_a_t_elle_bru.explanation: Small street in the City of London where the bakery in which the fire broke out on September 2, 1666 stood. It is the starting point of the Great Fire, remembered today by the Monument built close by.
Great medieval church that dominated the City of London. Destroyed in the fire of 1666, it was later replaced by the domed building seen today, a symbol of the city's reconstruction.

Senior official of the English navy, famous for the private diary he kept in the 1660s. His account of the fire of 1666, with its flames, flight and confusion, is one of the main eyewitness records of the event.
A gap created to stop a fire from advancing, here by demolishing buildings ahead of the flames. In 1666, the major firebreaks were organized too late to save the City of London.
Lord Mayor of London in 1666, that is, the chief magistrate of the City. Some historians blame him for delaying the demolitions that might have slowed the fire.

A contract under which an insurer pays for damage caused by fire in exchange for a premium. Almost nonexistent before 1666, it developed after the Great Fire of London and became a model still in use today.

course_252_la_vie_au_moyen_age_etait_ell.explanation: The share of children who die before their first birthday, or more broadly before adulthood, in a population. Very high in the Middle Ages, it drags average life expectancy down and feeds the false idea that adults died around 30.

The Church's calendar, which sets Sundays, the great feasts and the days devoted to saints throughout the year. In the Middle Ages it also set the pace of work: on certain days, ordinary labour was paused or forbidden.

A thick porridge of grains simmered for a long time, with beans, garden vegetables and, when available, scraps of meat added. Together with bread, it was the basis of the medieval peasant meal, far more varied than is often assumed.

Establishments where people came to wash in tubs of hot water, and sometimes to eat and relax. In some medieval towns they were so common that the authorities regulated and taxed them, proof that cleanliness mattered.

The means by which a town removes its waste and dirty water to keep its streets and water supply healthy. In the Middle Ages it remained very poor in crowded towns, which says nothing about the hygiene of each individual.

The first part of the Middle Ages, the centuries following the fall of the Western Roman Empire, up to around the year 1000. Life then differed greatly from life in the 14th century, a reminder that the medieval period was not one uniform block.

course_253_pourquoi_l_imprimerie_a_t_ell.explanation: A person who reproduced texts by hand, often a monk or a trained professional, before the arrival of printing. A scribe could spend months or years on a single manuscript, which made books rare and expensive.

German craftsman from Mainz who developed, around 1450, a printing system based on metal movable type. His press could turn out hundreds of copies of the same text and opened the age of the printed book in Europe.

Printing technique in which a text or image is carved in relief on a wooden block, then inked and pressed onto paper. Used in China and across Asia for centuries, it came long before Gutenberg's press.
Individual letters cast in metal that the printer arranges into words and pages, then takes apart to reuse. It was Gutenberg's key innovation: it avoided carving an entire block for every page.

German monk and professor of theology who challenged the Catholic Church in the early 16th century. His writings, printed as pamphlets and in German, spread far beyond his university and fed the Protestant Reformation.

Religious movement of the 16th century born of Martin Luther's challenge to the Catholic Church, which gave rise to the Protestant churches. Printing did not create it, but it let its ideas circulate on an unprecedented scale.
Nineteenth-century device that sends coded messages as electrical signals along a wire, in minutes rather than days. Like the printing press before it, it broke a bottleneck in communication.

course_254_qui_a_vendu_un_faux_vermeer_a.explanation: Dutch painter who became the most famous Vermeer forger of the 20th century. Tried in 1947 for selling a "Vermeer" to Göring, he escaped the treason charge by proving he had painted the picture himself.

Nazi leader, head of the German air force and avid collector of artworks, many of them looted across occupied Europe. He acquired Christ and the Adulteress believing it genuine and intended it for the gallery of his Carinhall estate.

Seventeenth-century Dutch painter, author of rare and highly sought-after interior scenes. The unproven hypothesis of an early "biblical phase" in his career was the gap through which Van Meegeren slipped his fakes.
Dutch art historian and recognized authority on Vermeer. He authenticated the Supper at Emmaus as an early Vermeer, and later refused to admit that it was a fake by Van Meegeren.

The first fully synthetic plastic, developed in the early 20th century. Mixed in liquid form with pigments, it hardened like old oil paint and let Van Meegeren's fakes pass the scientific analyses of the 1930s.

German banker based in the Netherlands and financial advisor to Göring. As the middleman in the sale of Christ and the Adulteress, he shipped the painting to Berlin when Van Meegeren had counted on selling it to a Dutch collector.

Göring's vast estate north of Berlin, where he gathered his art collection. The fake Vermeer was meant for its grand gallery, and it was among the Carinhall holdings that the painting was found at the end of the war.

course_255_comment_un_roman_a_t_il_sauve.explanation: Way of building born in the Paris region in the 12th century, recognizable by its ribbed vaults, flying buttresses and great windows. Notre-Dame, begun in 1163, is one of its first major examples, and Victor Hugo made it the symbol of all French Gothic.

Bishop of Paris in the 12th century, who started the construction of Notre-Dame in 1163, also financed by King Louis VII. His portrait appears with the king's on a tympanum of the cathedral's south-west entrance.
Natural island in the Seine at the center of Paris, the cradle of the city and the seat of royal and religious power for centuries. Notre-Dame stands there, facing the former palace of the kings.

Row of statues of Old Testament kings running across the main facade of Notre-Dame, above the portals. Mistaken for kings of France, they were beheaded in 1793, then replaced with new statues during Viollet-le-Duc's restoration.

Name given during the Revolution to churches turned into places celebrating revolutionary values, after worship was banned in 1793. Notre-Dame became one after serving as a warehouse, before reopening for worship in 1802.

French writer and poet with a passion for Gothic architecture. His novel Notre-Dame de Paris, published in 1831 after three years of studying the building, rallied readers to the cathedral and paved the way for the 1842 petition for its restoration.

Nineteenth-century French architect and great restorer of medieval monuments. With Jean-Baptiste Lassus, he led the restoration of Notre-Dame from 1845 to 1864, rebuilding the spire and the gallery of kings in an interpretation of the Middle Ages that is still debated.

course_256_pourquoi_a_t_on_peint_les_par.explanation: The largest chamber of the Lascaux cave, named after four great black bulls painted on its walls, the longest of them 5.2 meters. It is the most famous part of the site, the one that holds its largest figures.

The scientific name of our species, anatomically modern humans. So far, figurative art has been reliably recognized only in Homo sapiens: the paintings of Lascaux are thus a signature of the modern human mind, capable of language and abstract thought.

Humans of a species distinct from our own, who lived in Europe and western Asia before disappearing some tens of thousands of years ago. Signs and handprints are attributed to them in three caves in Spain, but no figurative art like that of Lascaux.

The last great period of the Old Stone Age, marked in Europe by the arrival of Homo sapiens, tools made of bone and reindeer antler and the first works of art. The Lascaux paintings date from its end, around 15,000 BC.

Hunter-gatherers of the late Upper Paleolithic, present in France, northern Spain, Switzerland, Germany, Belgium and southern Britain. Skilled at working bone and reindeer antler, they are most likely the makers of the Lascaux paintings.

A set of practices in which an intermediary, the shaman, makes contact with the world of spirits, often through trance and by taking on animal features. The bird-headed man of the Shaft led some researchers to think that Lascaux served this kind of rite.

A replica of the Lascaux cave opened to the public in 1983, twenty years after the original was closed, damaged by crowds of visitors and artificial lighting. It lets people see the paintings without putting the real cave at risk.

course_257_qui_a_fait_de_la_venus_de_mil.explanation: King of France from 1814 to 1824, brother of Louis XVI, restored to the throne after Napoleon's fall. He received the Venus de Milo brought back from Greece and gave it to the Louvre, which officially took it in 1821.

Officer in the French navy with a passion for archaeology, present on Milos in 1820. Sent to the site of the accidental dig, he drew the statue once it was uncovered: his sketch is the first record of the Venus as it was found.

Rectangular stone pillars topped with a bust, often that of the god Hermes, common in Greek gymnasiums and sanctuaries. Two herms flanked the Venus de Milo in its semicircular niche, according to Voutier's drawing.

Episode of Greek mythology alluded to in the Iliad: the Trojan prince Paris must name the most beautiful of the goddesses and chooses Aphrodite, who receives a golden apple. The hand holding an apple found on Milos would allude to that victory.

Sculptures from the Parthenon, the great temple of Athens, kept in London since the early 19th century. They were then seen as the peak of classical Greek art, and France dreamed of owning a treasure of the same rank in the Venus de Milo.

Athenian sculptor of the 5th century BC who directed the sculpted decoration of the Parthenon. French scholars of the 19th century compared the Venus de Milo with his works and tried to link her to him, to raise the statue to the rank of the greatest Greek masterpieces.

German archaeologist of the 19th century and specialist in Greek sculpture. In 1893 he published a long rebuttal, grounded in archaeology, of the French claim linking the Venus de Milo to Phidias, and part of his conclusions still holds today.

course_258_qui_s_est_vraiment_enrichi_pe.explanation: German-born pioneer who settled in 1839 in a California that still belonged to Mexico, dreaming of an agricultural empire, "New Helvetia," with orchards, a mill and a fort. Gold was discovered in 1848 at the sawmill he was having built at Coloma; he nonetheless died in poverty.

San Francisco merchant and newspaper publisher. After stocking his store with mining gear, he shouted the news of the gold discovery in the streets and became California's first millionaire by outfitting the prospectors, before dying poor.

Nickname of the roughly 100,000 people who arrived in California in 1849, the first big year of the Gold Rush. Coming mostly from the United States, but also from Latin America, Europe, Australia, Polynesia and China, they form the most famous wave of that migration.
The southern tip of South America, feared by sailors for its storms. Emigrants who reached California by sea had to sail around it: a journey of roughly 17,000 miles that took four to six months.

The narrow strip of land linking North America to South America. Crossing it shortened the journey to California, at the cost of exposure to yellow fever and malaria, before finding another ship to San Francisco.
Company founded in 1852 to carry the gold and mail of California's miners. It illustrates the fortunes built during the rush on services sold to the gold seekers rather than on gold itself.

course_259_pourquoi_amundsen_a_t_il_batt.explanation: Sea route linking the Atlantic to the Pacific through the icy waters of northern Canada. Amundsen was the first to sail all the way through it, from 1903 to 1906, and those years in the Arctic made him a seasoned polar explorer.

Inuit people of the Canadian Arctic, living notably on King William Island. Amundsen lived alongside them during his Northwest Passage voyage and learned from them fur clothing, dog driving and survival in extreme cold.

Norwegian polar ship whose name means "forward." In 1910 it left Norway with 97 dogs and 19 men, officially bound for the North Pole; Amundsen only announced the true destination, the South Pole, in Madeira.

British expedition led by Scott from 1901 aboard the ship Discovery, both scientific and exploratory. Its southern march of 1902, halted at 82°17' south, showed how poorly the British handled dogs and skis.

Disease caused by a lack of vitamin C, bringing exhaustion, bleeding gums and general weakness. Long the scourge of sailors and explorers deprived of fresh food, it struck Shackleton during the Discovery march of 1902.

Inlet on the Antarctic coast, cut into the great Ross Ice Shelf, where Amundsen set up his base in 1911. It put him about 60 miles closer to the Pole than Scott, at the cost of a route nobody had explored before.

course_260_d_ou_viennent_les_super_heros.explanation: Hero of Greek mythology, son of Zeus, famed for his colossal strength and his twelve labors; the Romans called him Hercules. He lends his strength to Shazam and, in Wonder Woman's story, he is the one who chains the Amazons.

A people of women warriors in Greek mythology, ruled by queens such as Hippolyta. William Moulton Marston made them Wonder Woman's family: enslaved by Hercules, they break free and found their own society.

American comic-book publisher that wanted a superhero of its own after the success of Superman. In 1940 it published Captain Marvel, the hero imagined by Bill Parker and drawn by C. C. Beck, in Whiz Comics #2.

Hero of the Old Testament gifted with superhuman strength, able to slay a lion with his bare hands. Jerry Siegel named him as a major influence on Superman, and the earliest comics compared the two strongmen directly.

American writer and editor who helped create the great Marvel heroes in the early 1960s, from the Fantastic Four to the Hulk. Looking for something "bigger than a god," he reinvented Thor with Larry Lieber and Jack Kirby in 1962.
Thor's hammer in Norse mythology, the signature weapon of the god of thunder. Stan Lee and Jack Kirby kept it when they brought Thor to Marvel in 1962, in Journey into Mystery #83.

course_261_a_t_on_vraiment_tout_perdu_da.explanation: A library founded by the Greek rulers of Egypt, the Ptolemies, which made Alexandria the foremost center of learning in antiquity. The course shows that its disappearance came from a long decline rather than from the fire of 48 BC.
A writing material made from the stems of a Nile marsh plant, cut into strips and pressed into sheets. Fragile in damp air, it explains why the scrolls of Alexandria crumbled away over time.
A dynasty of caliphs who ruled the Muslim world from Baghdad from 750 onward. Under their rule, scholars translated and extended Greek science, with figures such as Al-Khwarizmi and Ibn al-Haytham.

The name given to the translators gathered in Toledo, Spain, in the 12th century, who turned scientific texts from Arabic into Latin. Through them, the West rediscovered Ptolemy and the ancient science preserved in Arabic.

The temple of the god Serapis in Alexandria, which housed an annex library of the great library. Its destruction by a Christian mob in 391 fed the legend of a brutal annihilation of ancient knowledge.

The idea, spread in the 19th century by John William Draper and Andrew Dickson White, that religion and science are locked in permanent war. The supposed destruction of the Library of Alexandria became its favorite symbol.

A philosopher and mathematician of Alexandria, killed by a Christian mob in the early 5th century. The series Cosmos and the film Agora tied her death to the burning of the library, although the two events are separate.

course_262_comment_pompei_a_t_elle_dispa.explanation: The volcano that towers over the Bay of Naples in southern Italy, and one of the most famous in the world. Its eruption on October 24, AD 79 buried Pompeii under pumice and ash, and it has woken at least fifty times since Roman days.

A region of southern Italy around the Gulf of Naples, famous since antiquity for its mild climate and fertile soil. That wealth, born of the volcanic past of Vesuvius, drew farmers, merchants and rich Romans to Pompeii.

A Greek geographer of the age of the emperor Augustus, author of a Geography describing the world known to the Romans. The course names him among those who knew that Campania's rich soil came from the volcanic past of Vesuvius, without imagining the disaster.
A sauce made from fermented fish, a prized condiment in Roman cooking and an export product. Together with wine and woolen garments, it made Pompeii's commercial fortune before the eruption.
A light, porous volcanic rock formed when gas-filled lava cools suddenly. Hurled out by Vesuvius for twelve hours, it piled up on the roofs of Pompeii until they collapsed.

An avalanche of gas, ash and scorching rock that races down the slopes of a volcano at high speed when its eruption column collapses. At Pompeii, the fourth and fifth currents, at 250 to 300 °C, killed almost instantly those who had stayed.

course_263_a_quoi_servait_vraiment_la_ro.explanation: Envoy of Emperor Wu, sent westward in the 2nd century BC to forge alliances against the Xiongnu. His account of the riches of Central Asia and the horses of Fergana persuaded the emperor to open the way that would become the Silk Road.
A confederation of nomadic steppe peoples north of China whose raids threatened the Han empire. It was to find allies against them that Emperor Wu sent Zhang Qian westward in the 2nd century BC.

A fertile valley of Central Asia, famous in antiquity for its horses. Emperor Wu led two major campaigns there between 104 and 101 BC to seize these "Celestial Horses": the War of the Celestial Horses.

An epidemic that struck the Roman Empire from 165 to 180, under Marcus Aurelius, and which historians generally identify as smallpox. Brought back from the East by the legions, it decimated the population and weakened the imperial army.

The bacterium that causes plague, including its bubonic form. It lies behind the two greatest pandemics in the course, the Plague of Justinian from 541 and the Black Death of the 14th century, both of which came from Central Asia.

The period of relative stability imposed by the Mongol Empire across Eurasia in the 13th and 14th centuries, which secured and unified the trade routes. That same security sped the Black Death on its way from Central Asia to Europe.
A phrase coined by the historian Emmanuel Le Roy Ladurie in 1973 to describe how long-isolated regions pooled their diseases as trade connected them. The Silk Road is one of the first great examples.

course_264_qui_a_vraiment_construit_les_.explanation: A mid-level inspector under Khufu, in charge of a crew of about forty men. His logbooks, found in 2013, are the oldest inscribed papyri from Egypt and describe the shipping of limestone to Giza.
Pharaoh of Egypt's Old Kingdom, about 4,500 years ago. The Great Pyramid of Giza, the tallest of the three, was raised for him, with more than two million stone blocks.
A city in southern Egypt, on the Nile, known for its granite quarries. The beams of Khufu's burial chamber, up to 80 tons each, were hauled from there over 900 kilometers.
A rocky plateau at the edge of the desert, near Cairo, where the three great pyramids stand. Chosen for its abundant limestone, it also held the town of the construction workers.
An ancient Egyptian harbor on the Red Sea coast. In 2013, a French team discovered the papyri of the inspector Merer there, sealed in a rock gallery.
Fine limestone quarries on the Nile, across from Giza. Their blocks were used for the gleaming outer casing of the Great Pyramid, which Merer's crew shipped by boat.

An American archaeologist who has been excavating the workers' town at the foot of the Giza Plateau since 1988. His finds show workers who were housed, fed and well treated, far from the image of slaves.

course_265_pourquoi_les_spartiates_etaie.explanation: The legendary lawgiver of Sparta, active according to tradition in the 9th or 8th century BC. The whole organization of the city, from the two kings to the communal meals, is credited to him, though historians see centuries of development.
The sanctuary of Apollo in central Greece, where a priestess delivered the god's answers. Its sacred endorsement, the "Great Rhetra," is said to have legitimized the laws of Lycurgus in Spartan eyes.
The five magistrates of Sparta, elected each year to watch over the city and its kings. They were the ones who formally declared war on the helots every year.

The state education of Spartan boys, who left their families at the age of seven. Barefoot and dressed in a single garment all year, they learned the endurance and obedience that made the city's reputation.
The modest communal meals that Spartan citizens ate together every day. Each man had to pay his share: one who could no longer pay lost his citizenship, which slowly emptied the city of its Equals.

The battle formation of Greek foot soldiers, packed in close ranks with shields locked together. Sparta's heavy infantry, in red tunics and with bronze shields, made it the most disciplined army in the Greek world.
The enslaved population of Sparta, who farmed the citizens' land and vastly outnumbered them. Holding them down was the army's vital task; their liberation in Messenia in 371 BC ruined the city.
Secret units of young Spartans sent into the countryside to kill helots and keep fear alive. They completed the war the ephors declared each year on the enslaved population.

course_266_pourquoi_y_a_t_il_du_cobalt_d.explanation: Vast country in Central Africa, rich in copper and cobalt, especially in the Katanga region. It supplies about three-quarters of the world's cobalt, almost always as a by-product of its copper mines.

American physicist and chemist who found in 1980, at Oxford, with Koichi Mizushima, that lithium cobalt oxide works as a cathode. That discovery made possible the lithium-ion battery Sony brought to market in 1991.

Mechanism by which ions slide between the layers of a sheet-like material, then back out, without destroying its structure. This is how lithium enters and leaves the cobalt cathode with every charge and discharge.

One of the two electrodes of a battery, the one that takes in the lithium ions when the battery discharges. In this course, it is the cobalt oxide part that gives the lithium-ion battery its stability.
Chain reaction in which a battery's heat breaks down its cathode, frees oxygen and feeds a fire that produces even more heat. This is why a lithium battery fire cannot be smothered.

Lithium-ion battery whose cathode is made of lithium iron phosphate, with no cobalt. It runs cooler and costs less, but stores less energy for the same weight, which is why it is found mostly in cars.
Small-scale mining, dug and sorted by hand, without machines or protection. In the Congo, part of the cobalt comes from it, in unsafe conditions and in places with child labor.

course_267_qui_a_tue_le_premier_cable|Va.explanation: Island off the southwest coast of Ireland, the European end of the 1858 transatlantic cable. It is where Thomson handed over to Whitehouse on August 5, and where he returned to investigate after the line died.

course_267_qui_a_tue_le_premier_cable|Wi.explanation: Electrician of the Atlantic Telegraph Company, with no training in physics. He disputed Thomson's calculations, drove up to 2,000 volts into the 1858 cable to force the signals through, faked the tape of the first message and was dismissed.

course_267_qui_a_tue_le_premier_cable|At.explanation: British company founded to lay the first telegraph cable between Ireland and Newfoundland. Its directors signed the very first transatlantic message, and its board ran the inquiry after the line died in September 1858.

course_267_qui_a_tue_le_premier_cable|Wi.explanation: Scottish physicist, the future Lord Kelvin, scientific adviser to the 1858 cable. He predicted retardation, called for a thicker copper core, read the signals on his mirror galvanometer and reconstructed the causes of the failure.

course_267_qui_a_tue_le_premier_cable|re.explanation: Effect predicted by Thomson: in a long submarine cable, electrical signals spread out and slow down instead of arriving sharp. Whitehouse denied it after tests on buried lines, which do not behave like an underwater cable.

course_267_qui_a_tue_le_premier_cable|mi.explanation: Thomson's instrument, in which a tiny suspended mirror deflects a beam of light at the slightest current. Sensitive enough to read the faint pulses coming from the other side of the Atlantic, where Whitehouse's equipment registered nothing.

course_267_qui_a_tue_le_premier_cable|Gr.explanation: Huge steamship chartered to lay a new transatlantic cable. It lost the cable in mid-ocean in 1865, then achieved the lasting link between Ireland and Newfoundland in 1866.

course_268_pourquoi_le_violet_est_il_la_.explanation: Sea snail with a spiny shell, found in the eastern Mediterranean and along the Atlantic coast of Morocco. A gland under its shell secretes the liquid from which Tyrian purple is made: thousands of snails are needed for a few grams of dye.

Port city of Phoenicia, on the coast of modern Lebanon and a great trading center of the ancient world. The murex snails gathered off its shores gave Tyrian purple its name, and the Phoenicians were producing the dye there by about 1200 BC.

Blue dye of plant origin, the blue of denim and one of the cheapest dyes in history. Its molecule is the base of Tyrian purple: attach two bromine atoms to it and ordinary blue becomes the purple of emperors.

Chemical element that is very abundant in seawater. Fixed onto the indigo molecule, its atoms make the purple: one gives violet, two give the reddish purple of the Romans, and sunlight can knock them back off and push the color toward blue.

Ritual blue of Judaism, the color of the fringes sewn onto certain garments. It comes from the same snail as Tyrian purple: when light strips bromine atoms from the molecule, the shade slides from purple toward this blue.

Roman writer and naturalist of the 1st century, author of a vast encyclopedia, the Natural History. He describes how purple was made, but his recipe is incomplete: it is one of the texts the chemist who got the vat running again in 1998 had to fill in.

Electronic component that lets a current through or blocks it, the basic building block of microchips. Evaporated into a thin film, the Tyrian purple molecule, which conducts electricity and carries both kinds of charge, becomes one.

course_269_pourquoi_personne_ne_sourit_s.explanation: A dark room or box with a small hole through which light throws an upside-down image of the outside world onto the opposite wall. Known since antiquity, it shows an image without being able to keep it: the starting point of photography.

French inventor who, in 1826, captured the oldest surviving photograph from nature, the view from the window of his house at Le Gras. His bitumen process needed hours of exposure, which ruled out any portrait.

The first photographic process released to the public, developed by Louis Daguerre: a silver-plated sheet sensitized with iodine vapor, developed over mercury and fixed in hot salt water. It cut the exposure from hours to minutes, and France gave it to the world in 1839.

The length of time the plate receives light to form the image. Hours with Niépce, a few minutes with Daguerre, a few seconds by the 1850s: it is what people wrongly blame for the serious faces in old portraits.

American from Philadelphia who, in 1839, made the oldest surviving photographic self-portrait by posing outside his family's shop. Hair untidy and arms folded, he is not smiling: the portrait kept its rules.

Art historian and author of a history of the smile. He points out that in older painting a wide smile signaled madness, drunkenness or stupidity, and that dentistry, more than shyness, is what finally opened mouths in front of the lens.
A photograph taken in an instant, without a prepared pose, made possible by fast, cheap cameras. It took photography out of the studio and, by the 1920s, made the smile the expected face.

course_270_pourquoi_la_yougoslavie_a_t_e.displayTerm: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes
course_270_pourquoi_la_yougoslavie_a_t_e.explanation: State proclaimed on 1 December 1918 in the Balkans, uniting three nations that spoke almost the same language. Renamed Yugoslavia in 1929, it was born as a survival union against its neighbors Italy and Austria.

Communist leader of Yugoslavia from the end of World War II until his death in 1980. A strong and respected leader on good terms with both West and East, he was the glue of a federation that came apart after him.

Serbian politician who rose to power in Belgrade in the late 1980s by stirring up Serbian national feeling. A central figure of the Yugoslav wars, he embodies the rise of the nationalisms that tore the federation apart.

Mass execution of Bosnian civilians in July 1995, in eastern Bosnia, by Serbian forces. It is the only event of the Yugoslav wars that the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia has ruled a genocide.

Offensive launched by the Croatian army in August 1995, a month after Srebrenica, against areas populated by Serbs. Carl Bildt, the European Union's special envoy, described it as one of the most efficient acts of ethnic cleansing in history.

course_270_pourquoi_la_yougoslavie_a_t_e.displayTerm: International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia
course_270_pourquoi_la_yougoslavie_a_t_e.explanation: Court created by UN Security Council Resolution 827 to judge the crimes committed during the Yugoslav wars. Based in The Hague, this special tribunal recognized only one genocide, Srebrenica.

The expulsion or elimination of a population from a territory because of its origin, to make that territory ethnically homogeneous. The term became common during the Yugoslav wars, when each side drove out civilians of the other origin.

course_271_pourquoi_les_etats_unis_sont_.explanation: A state whose military, economic and cultural power far exceeds that of all others and reaches the whole planet. The word was applied to the United States for the first time in the aftermath of World War II.

International institution born of the Bretton Woods conference in 1944 to stabilize currencies and lend to countries in difficulty. The dollar holds a central place in it, which strengthened the financial weight of the United States after 1945.

The North Atlantic Treaty Organization, a military alliance binding the United States, Canada and Western European countries after World War II. It gave Washington a web of allies across the whole European continent.
The idea that in the United States anyone can succeed through hard work, whatever their origin. This myth drew millions of immigrants, whose energy fed the country's industry, research and education.

American political scientist who coined the notion of soft power in 1990, in the journal Foreign Policy. In his view, a country also dominates through the appeal of its culture and ideas, not only through military force.
A country's ability to get what it wants through the appeal of its culture, values and way of life, without threat or reward. After the Cold War, it became the cornerstone of American dominance.

Confrontation without direct war between the United States and the Soviet Union, from the end of World War II to the early 1990s. The Soviet Union stood up to the Americans before exhausting itself on too many fronts.

A group of eight prestigious private universities in the northeastern United States, including Harvard, Yale and Princeton. These institutions attract students from all over the world and are part of American soft power.

course_272_pourquoi_la_coree_est_elle_co.explanation: The last royal dynasty of Korea, which ruled the whole peninsula for more than five centuries, until 1910. Its fall opened nearly forty years of Japanese rule, then the partition of the country in 1945.

The line of latitude chosen in 1945 by two American colonels to split Korea between a Soviet zone in the north and an American zone in the south. Meant as a temporary border, it still separates the two Koreas.

Confrontation without direct war between the United States and the Soviet Union, from 1945 to the early 1990s. In Korea, it turned a temporary partition into a permanent division and led to a real war in 1950.

The official name of South Korea, a state proclaimed in 1948 in the American zone, with Seoul as its capital. A democracy allied with the United States, it has become a major economic and technological power.

The official name of North Korea, a communist regime proclaimed in 1948 in the Soviet zone. A dictatorship isolated both internationally and economically, it imposes long military service and develops nuclear weapons.

Conflict triggered on 25 June 1950 by North Korea's invasion of the South, backed by the Soviet Union and China. The fighting stopped in 1953 without a peace treaty, leaving the country officially at war.
A strip of territory established in 1953 along the 38th parallel, where no armed forces may be stationed. It still separates the two Koreas, whose armies face each other on either side of the line.
The web formed by the armed forces, the arms industry and the politicians who vote their budgets, whose interests reinforce one another. The Korean War sent its funding soaring in the United States.

course_273_pourquoi_la_suisse_n_est_elle.explanation: The status of a state that takes no part in wars between other states and enters no military alliance, while keeping the right to defend itself. In Switzerland it has been a recognized doctrine since 1815 and the foundation of the country's foreign policy.

A conference of the great European powers held in 1814-1815 to reorganize the continent after the Napoleonic Wars. It recognized Switzerland's perpetual neutrality, which the country has never abandoned since.

International treaties signed in 1907 in The Hague, in the Netherlands, to set the rules of war. They codify the rights and duties of neutral states, on land and at sea, and remain a major source of international law.

course_273_pourquoi_la_suisse_n_est_elle.displayTerm: International Committee of the Red Cross
course_273_pourquoi_la_suisse_n_est_elle.explanation: A humanitarian organization founded in Geneva in 1863 to protect the victims of armed conflict, and the origin of the Red Cross movement. Its Geneva headquarters embody the humanitarian face of Swiss neutrality.
A system that makes military service compulsory by law. In Switzerland every man must serve at least 245 days from the age of 18, on pain of prison, which makes the army a pillar of armed neutrality.

A rule that forbids Swiss banks from revealing the identity and assets of their clients. It drew German and Jewish fortunes to the country after 1918, then dubious funds, and feeds the criticism of neutrality's dark side.

The North Atlantic Treaty Organization, a military alliance founded in 1949 around the United States and Western Europe, in which an attack on one member commits all the others. Switzerland has never belonged to it, but the debate over closer ties divides the country.

course_274_peut_on_modifier_l_adn_d_un_e.explanation: A segment of DNA that carries the instruction for making a protein or running a function of the body, inherited from our parents. It is the unit the CRISPR scissors can switch off, correct or replace.
A defense system bacteria use against viruses, turned in 2012 into a tool for cutting DNA at a chosen spot. It made possible the first gene-editing treatments approved in 2023.
The complete DNA of an organism, written with the four bases A, T, C and G. A single wrong letter in that long text can be enough to cause a genetic disease.
An inherited blood disorder that bends red blood cells into a sickle shape. It was the first disease targeted by a CRISPR-based medicine, approved in the United Kingdom in 2023.

A form of hemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen in the blood, produced before birth and then replaced by the adult form. The 2023 CRISPR treatment restarts its production to make up for the faulty hemoglobin.
A technique that brings an egg and a sperm cell together in the laboratory, then implants the resulting embryo in the womb. Its arrival gave birth to the phrase "designer baby," long before CRISPR.
Changing the DNA of reproductive cells, meaning sperm, eggs or early embryos, so that the change is passed on to every following generation. It is currently banned in every country in the world.

course_275_que_peut_on_vraiment_lire_dan.explanation: The complete DNA of a person, written as a sequence of the four nucleotides A, T, C and G. It is this unique genetic blueprint that we "read" in search of tastes, disease risks and origins.
A segment of DNA that carries the instruction for making a protein, which in turn builds and runs our cells. Our visible traits come from genes, and recent research links some of them to personality.

A slightly different version of the same gene, inherited from our parents, which sets individuals apart from one another. Some variants weigh on our preferences, others raise the risk of a disease such as breast cancer.
Carrying genes that raise the probability of developing a trait or a disease, without making it certain. A genetic risk of depression, for instance, does not mean you will suffer from it.
Two genes whose inherited variants predispose some women to early-onset breast cancer. Spotting them with a test makes earlier screening, closer monitoring or preventive treatment possible.

The analysis of a person's DNA in search of variants linked to a disease risk. It makes early action possible, through earlier screening or preventive treatment, which can save lives and reduce medical costs.

The large peninsula in the southwest of Europe, today Spain and Portugal. Its present-day inhabitants still carry genetic traces of the people who came from North Africa between 700 and 1200 AD, just as written history recounts.

course_276_pourquoi_les_antibiotiques_ce.explanation: Said of an antibiotic that kills bacteria outright, by attacking their cell wall or their contents, as opposed to a bacteriostatic one, which only blocks their multiplication. In both cases, a bacterium that learns to resist makes the drug useless.

The ability a bacterium acquires to survive an antibiotic that would normally kill it or block its growth. Born of the massive use of these drugs, it is making some common infections harder and harder to treat.

Proteins lodged in the bacterium's envelope that push toxic substances, antibiotics included, back outside before they can act. They are one of the defenses that selection by antibiotics has favored in resistant bacteria.

The passing of genes from one bacterium to another without reproduction, unlike the inheritance handed down when a cell divides. It lets a resistance gene spread very quickly through a population of bacteria.

Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, a bacterium that has become insensitive to many widely used antibiotics, hence its nickname of superbug. It shows how massive antibiotic use left the field open to the most resistant strains.
