The World Health Organization, the United Nations agency in charge of public health across the planet. It ranks antimicrobial resistance among the three biggest health threats in the world.

A body-wide infection, in which bacteria and the body's reaction against them spread through the whole organism and put life at risk. Without effective antibiotics, a simple infected wound could lead to it.

course_277_les_sanctions_evitent_elles_v.explanation: Non-military pressure applied by one or more states against a government: a trade embargo, frozen assets, a ban on selling certain equipment. Presented as an alternative to war, in Iraq they hit civilians first.

The United Nations body in charge of keeping the peace, whose resolutions are binding on every member state. It imposed the embargo on Iraq in August 1990 and created the Oil-for-Food Programme in 1995.

President of Iraq from 1979 to 2003. His invasion of Kuwait in August 1990 triggered the UN embargo and then the Gulf War; his regime rode out the sanctions and even tightened its grip on a population dependent on rations.

The 1991 conflict in which an international coalition drove the Iraqi army out of Kuwait. The bombing destroyed power stations and water systems, but left Saddam Hussein in power and the embargo in place.

A program created by Security Council Resolution 986 in April 1995. It allowed Iraq to sell oil under UN supervision to buy food, medicine and civilian supplies; it eased shortages without replacing a working economy.

A concept from political theory for violence with no visible author, built into the rules and frameworks of decision-making themselves. According to Jürgen Habermas, it narrows in advance the options that can be debated: here, the choice between sanctions and war.

course_278_pourquoi_les_accords_climatiq.explanation: Gases such as carbon dioxide or methane that trap the sun's heat in the atmosphere and warm the planet. Cutting their emissions is the purpose of every climate agreement, from Kyoto to Paris.
A treaty adopted in 1997 that set legally binding emissions targets for industrialized countries, with penalties for exceeding them. The United States never ratified it and Canada withdrew in 2012.

A situation in which everyone has an interest in letting others make an effort that will benefit all, so that nobody acts. On climate, each state waits for its neighbors to cut emissions in its place.

A treaty adopted in 2015 in which each country sets its own reduction goals, renewed every five years, and reports on its progress. Its compliance committee can penalize no one, and the United States left it in 2026.

A 1987 treaty requiring the ban of chemicals that destroy the ozone layer, with financial help to convert factories. Nearly 99% of the targeted substances had been phased out by 2023: an example of an environmental agreement that was enforced.
A state's power to decide alone, with no higher authority, what happens on its territory. Enforcing climate agreements more strictly would require states to accept limits on part of it.

course_279_pourquoi_accepter_une_armee_e.explanation: The exclusive authority a state claims over its territory and its population, with no higher power above it. Foreign bases put it under strain: a sovereign state accepts another power's army on its own soil.

A sheltered harbor near Oran, on the Algerian coast, occupied by France from 1830 and turned into a modern naval base in the 1930s. After independence in 1962, France kept the right to stay there for fifteen years.

Agreements signed in 1962 between France and Algerian representatives, ending the Algerian War and opening the way to independence. They recognized Mers el-Kébir as Algerian territory while leaving the base to France for fifteen years.

A 1940 exchange between Washington and London: fifty old American destroyers for 99-year leases on bases in Britain's Atlantic colonies. It opened another empire's possessions to the American military before the United States even entered the war.

The rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union from the end of World War II to 1991, without direct fighting between them. Each side tried to draw former colonies into its sphere of influence, notably by setting up bases there.

The name the United States gave to the global military campaign launched after the attacks of September 11, 2001. It relies on the network of American bases to pursue suspects across national borders.
An American naval base in Cuba, leased since 1903 in the wake of the Spanish-American War. In 2002 the United States opened a detention camp there for people captured abroad in the war on terror.

course_280_pourquoi_le_dollar_domine_t_i.explanation: Holdings of foreign currencies that a central bank keeps to pay for imports, repay external debts and weather crises. In early 2026, about 57% of the reserves reported worldwide are still in dollars.

A meeting of 44 Allied delegations in New Hampshire, in July 1944, to set the monetary rules of the postwar world. It pegged currencies to the dollar, the dollar to gold, and created the International Monetary Fund.

One of the most influential British economists of the 20th century, who negotiated for Britain at Bretton Woods. He proposed an international unit of account, the bancor, and pressure on surplus countries, both of which the Americans set aside.

An international unit of account devised by Keynes to settle debts between countries without going through a national currency. The plan was dropped at Bretton Woods in favor of a fund lending national currencies, with the dollar at the center.

The institution created by the Bretton Woods agreements to lend currencies to countries struggling to pay their way. The IMF now publishes the statistics on world foreign exchange reserves cited in the course.

A system in which a currency's value moves freely with supply and demand on the market, instead of being fixed against another currency. The major currencies switched to it in 1973, after the dollar's conversion into gold ended.
Debt securities issued by the American government, easy to buy and sell, that pay interest. Foreign central banks park a large share of their dollar reserves in them, which finances U.S. borrowing.

course_281_comment_meurt_une_etoile|nucl.explanation: A reaction in which the nuclei of light atoms, such as hydrogen, join to form heavier nuclei, such as helium, releasing enormous amounts of energy. It is what makes stars shine, and its shutdown, when the fuel runs out, is what triggers their death.

course_281_comment_meurt_une_etoile|red.explanation: A stage in the life of a star whose core has used up its hydrogen: the outer layers swell enormously and cool down, which gives the reddish color. The Sun will go through this phase in about 5 billion years.

course_281_comment_meurt_une_etoile|plan.explanation: A glowing cloud of gas formed by the outer layers that a star like the Sun throws off at the end of its life. Despite its name, inherited from early telescopes that saw it as round like a planet, it has nothing to do with planets.

course_281_comment_meurt_une_etoile|whit.explanation: The hot, dense core left behind by a low-mass star after it has shed its outer layers. About the size of Earth, it keeps a large share of the star's mass and shines only from its leftover heat, before slowly cooling down.

course_281_comment_meurt_une_etoile|supe.explanation: A gigantic explosion that follows the collapse of a massive star's core, once its iron core can no longer supply energy. It blasts much of the star into space and scatters the heavy elements that will go on to form other worlds.

course_281_comment_meurt_une_etoile|neut.explanation: What remains of a massive star's collapsed core after a supernova, when that core is not heavy enough to become a black hole. Its density is extreme: an enormous mass packed into an object no bigger than a city.

course_281_comment_meurt_une_etoile|blac.explanation: An object formed when the core of a very massive star collapses with nothing left to stop it. Its gravity is so strong that not even light can escape. The first image of a black hole, the one in the galaxy M87, dates from 2019.

course_282_que_se_passerait_il_si_un_sup.explanation: A volcano capable of a colossal eruption, throwing out more than 1,000 km³ of rock, ash and gas, enough to fill 400 million Olympic swimming pools. Its effects are not local: ash across a continent, gas high in the atmosphere and a cooler climate.

A huge basin-shaped depression that forms when the ground collapses above a store of magma emptied by a great eruption. It is the mark supervolcanoes leave behind, in place of the cone people usually picture.

A national park in the western United States that sits on the caldera of a supervolcano. Its geysers and hot springs betray the magma deep below, and its earthquakes, ground swelling and gas emissions are monitored around the clock.

An avalanche of scorching gas, ash and blocks of rock that races down the sides of a volcano at very high speed. It destroys almost everything in its path and is the deadliest threat near a major eruption, far more than lava.

Dust made of tiny, sharp fragments of rock, minerals and volcanic glass, nothing like the soft ash of a wood fire. Even in a thin layer, it damages engines, contaminates water and disrupts road and air transport.

A sharp-smelling gas released by volcanic eruptions. Thrown high into the atmosphere, it turns into fine particles that reflect part of the sunlight back into space and temporarily cool the planet: this is the volcanic winter.

A volcano in the Philippines whose June 1991 eruption, far smaller than a supereruption, lowered the global average temperature by about 0.5°C for close to two years. It serves as the reference for measuring how volcanoes affect the climate.

course_283_qu_y_a_t_il_vraiment_dans_un_.explanation: A toughened glass made of silicon, aluminum and oxygen that protects the screen of many smartphones. A chemical treatment replaces the small sodium atoms at the surface with larger potassium atoms, which compresses the glass and slows down cracks.

A rare material that conducts electricity while staying transparent. Laid down in a very thin layer beneath the cover glass, it lets a touchscreen detect a finger through a change in the electrical signal, without hiding the image displayed underneath.

A chemical element that is very abundant in the Earth's crust. Once purified, it forms the base of electronic chips: the tiny circuits of a smartphone's processor and memory are etched into this material.

A very light metal at the heart of rechargeable batteries, where it stores and releases energy together with graphite. It is produced mainly in Australia, Chile, China and Argentina, notably by evaporating brines in salt deserts.

A family of metals, such as neodymium, with exceptional magnetic properties. In a smartphone, they are used to make the tiny but very powerful magnets of the speakers, microphones and vibration motor.

A metal essential to smartphone batteries. Most of the world's production is mined in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, before being refined and turned into components on other continents, which makes its supply sensitive.

Discarded electrical and electronic devices, from phones to computers. The world produced 62 million metric tons of it in 2022, of which barely more than 20% was collected and recycled, even though it is full of reusable metals.

course_284_pourquoi_mars_est_elle_devenu.explanation: The force exerted by the weight of the air on a surface. On Mars it is less than 1% of Earth's, too little for liquid water to remain stable on the surface: it freezes or evaporates.
The warming of a planet by the gases in its atmosphere, which hold back part of the heat received from the Sun. The thick atmosphere of early Mars kept its surface warm enough for liquid water.
The region of magnetic influence that surrounds some planets and deflects charged particles coming from the Sun. Mars lost its own, which left its atmosphere exposed to the solar wind.
A continuous stream of charged particles thrown out by the Sun across the solar system. With no magnetic field to deflect it, it strikes the upper atmosphere of Mars and knocks gases away into space.
The outer rocky layer of a planet, the one you can touch at the surface. On Mars, part of the ancient water reacted with its rocks and remains locked there inside minerals.
Thick layers of ice covering the poles of a planet. Those of Mars still hold large amounts of frozen water today, part of the water the planet never lost.

course_285_pourquoi_la_lune_s_eloigne_t_.explanation: The American space program that sent astronauts to the Moon between 1969 and 1972. They left reflectors there: by timing laser pulses bounced back by these panels, scientists measure the Earth-Moon distance and its increase of 3.8 cm a year.

The pulling force that every massive body exerts on others, stronger the closer you are to it. The Moon's gravity pulls harder on the side of Earth facing it, which lifts the oceans and sets the whole mechanism of the tides in motion.

Slight swellings of the oceans, one facing the Moon and the other on the opposite side, created by the difference in the Moon's pull from one side of Earth to the other. Carried ahead by Earth's rotation, they pull the Moon forward and slowly push it away.

The curved path a body follows around another under the effect of gravity: the Moon completes its own around Earth in about a month. The energy supplied by the tides gradually moves it onto a slightly wider orbit.

The energy a body has because it spins on its axis, as Earth does once every 24 hours. Through the tides, our planet hands a minute share of it to the Moon: the Moon moves away, Earth spins a little more slowly, and a day was once shorter.

The event in which the Moon, passing between Earth and the Sun, hides the Sun's disk completely for a few minutes. It is only possible because the Sun, 400 times wider than the Moon, is also 400 times farther away. In 600 million years, the Moon will look too small.

course_286_comment_a_t_on_evite_la_famin.explanation: A set of agricultural advances from the middle of the 20th century: higher-yielding varieties of wheat, corn and rice, irrigation, fertilizers and transport. Led by Norman Borlaug in Mexico and then India, it allowed many countries to feed themselves and kept the world famine predicted for 1960 at bay.

A series of dust storms that ravaged the American Great Plains in the 1930s, after years of drought and intensive plowing. They ruined thousands of farms and, together with the Great Depression, fed the fear of running out that still haunted America in the 1950s.

The sharp rise in births in Western countries after World War II, from 1945 to the early 1960s. This population surge fed the fear that traditional farming could no longer feed a fast-growing world population.

An American philanthropic organization created by the Rockefeller family, active in public health and agriculture. Partnered with the Mexican government in the MAP program, it employed Norman Borlaug and funded the seed research that gave birth to the Green Revolution.

American agronomist nicknamed the "Father of the Green Revolution." In Mexico with the Rockefeller Foundation, and then in India, he developed higher-yielding varieties of wheat and corn suited to varied climates, which turned Mexico into a wheat exporter in under ten years.

A region of southeastern Nigeria that seceded in 1967, shortly after the country's independence. The Nigerian government blocked its access to the ports: the famine that followed, widely photographed, fixed the image of children with swollen bellies in people's minds.

A campaign launched by Mao in 1958 to industrialize China at breakneck speed, with makeshift blast furnaces in the countryside and grain collection reorganized by the state. It threw the countryside into chaos and caused a gigantic famine: nearly 50 million deaths between 1958 and 1962.

course_287_pourquoi_a_t_on_ravitaille_be.explanation: The supplying of a population by plane when the land routes are cut. The Berlin airlift, run by the Western powers for fifteen months from 1948, fed West Berlin during the Soviet blockade and became the first great humanitarian operation of the Cold War.

The confrontation without direct war between the United States and the Soviet Union, from the late 1940s to 1991, each defending its own political and economic model. Berlin, cut in two in the heart of the Soviet zone, became its first symbol with the blockade and the airlift of 1948.

Stalin's closure, in 1948, of the railways and waterways linking West Berlin to the Western zones, to drive out the Americans, the British and the French. It failed thanks to the airlift and ended when Stalin ordered the transit routes reopened.

The victorious coalition of World War II, led by the United States, the United Kingdom, the Soviet Union and France. After 1945, these four powers divided Germany and Berlin into occupation zones, before the American-Soviet rivalry split them apart.

Joseph Stalin, master of the Soviet Union from the late 1920s until his death in 1953. In 1948, he rejected in advance the Western powers' decisions on Germany and ordered the Berlin Blockade, which he had to lift when the maneuver failed.

The nickname of American pilot Gail Halvorsen, who dropped candy tied to handkerchief parachutes for the children of West Berlin during the airlift. His images went around the world and won America the goodwill of future allies.

A wall built in 1961 by the East German government to stop its people from fleeing to West Berlin. It cut the city in two for 28 years, until 9 November 1989, when Berliners crossed it and then tore it down with hammers: the Cold War was drawing to a close.

course_288_que_s_est_il_passe_a_bhopal_l.explanation: A nuclear power plant in Pennsylvania, in the United States, where a reactor suffered a partial meltdown in 1979, with no direct victims but amid great panic. Together with Chernobyl, this accident brackets Bhopal and fed distrust of industrial technology.

A nuclear power plant in Ukraine, then part of the Soviet Union, where a reactor exploded in 1986 and contaminated a vast region of Europe. Coming two years after Bhopal, the accident confirmed the fear of technology running out of control.

A title borne by Muslim princesses and female rulers in India. In Bhopal, Begum Shah Jahan governed the state in the 19th century and built the Taj Mahal Palace, which bears the same name as the celebrated mausoleum in Agra.

An American chemical group whose Indian subsidiary, Union Carbide India Limited (UCIL), built the Bhopal pesticide plant in 1969. After the 1984 leak, the company paid $470 million to the victims in 1989, but its leaders escaped prosecution in India.

The rise of intensive farming from the 1960s onward, based on new seeds, irrigation, fertilizers and pesticides. In India, it sent demand for agricultural chemicals soaring, which justified building the Bhopal plant.

A highly toxic gas, MIC for short, used to make the pesticide Sevin. It attacks the lungs, the eyes and the digestive system. More than 30 tons of it escaped from the Bhopal plant on the night of 3 December 1984.

course_289_pourquoi_l_urss_s_est_elle_ef.explanation: Leader of the Soviet Union from 1985 until his resignation on December 25, 1991. Brought to power to revive an exhausted country, he launched glasnost and perestroika, an opening that quickly slipped out of the Kremlin's control.

The rivalry between the United States and the USSR from 1945 to 1991, with no direct fighting between the two superpowers but with proxy conflicts in Korea, Vietnam and Afghanistan. It ended with the dissolution of the Soviet Union.

The Russian revolutionary movement led by Lenin, which won the struggle for power after the tsar was overthrown in 1917. It was the Bolsheviks who founded the USSR in 1922 and installed the communist regime the country kept for nearly seventy years.

The military alliance the USSR formed with the communist countries of Eastern Europe during the Cold War. Its members rose up from Poland onward in 1980 and cast off their leaders in 1989, stripping Moscow of its closest allies.

A Russian word meaning openness or transparency. The policy Gorbachev launched in 1985 to tell the truth about the state of the country and free up public speech. It also freed the demands of the republics, which the Kremlin could no longer contain.

A Russian word meaning restructuring. The reform Gorbachev launched in 1985 to reorganize the Soviet economy and state. Carried out alongside glasnost, it weakened central power instead of reviving it.

The agreement signed on December 21, 1991 by the leaders of the Soviet republics to end the Union. It designated Russia as the successor to the USSR; four days later, Gorbachev resigned and the Soviet flag left the Kremlin.

President of Russia at the time of the dissolution of the USSR. Gorbachev's resignation on December 25, 1991 transferred power to him and made the Russia he led the official heir of the vanished Soviet Union.

course_290_comment_les_etats_unis_ont_il.explanation: The rivalry between the United States and the USSR from 1945 to 1991, with no direct fighting between the two superpowers but with proxy wars and constant technological competition. The race to the Moon is one of its most closely followed episodes.

An impromptu, filmed exchange in 1959 between American vice president Richard Nixon and Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev, in the model kitchen of an American exhibition in Moscow. Each praised his country's way of life, at times in a comic tone.

The name of the first artificial satellites, launched by the Soviet Union from 1957 onward. Sputnik 1 opened the Space Race; Sputnik 2 carried the dog Laika, the first living creature placed in orbit around the Earth.
Soviet cosmonaut who, in 1961, became the first human to fly in space. His feat confirmed the USSR's lead and pushed the United States to set itself an even more ambitious goal: the Moon.

The American space program of the 1960s that sent a total of 16 astronauts into flight to master piloting and docking between spacecraft. It ended in 1966 and directly prepared the Apollo missions to the Moon.

A vast dark plain on the near side of the Moon, chosen as the landing site for Apollo 11. It is where Armstrong and Aldrin touched down on July 20, 1969 and took humanity's first steps on another world.

The first space program carried out jointly by the United States and the Soviet Union, in 1975. An Apollo spacecraft and a Soyuz spacecraft docked in orbit and their crews shook hands, opening the era of cooperation in space.

course_291_l_esclavage_americain_a_t_il_.explanation: The war of 1861 to 1865 between the Northern states, which stayed in the Union, and the slaveholding Southern states, which formed the Confederacy. The Union's victory led to the official abolition of slavery by the Thirteenth Amendment.

President of the United States during the Civil War, whose election drove the Southern states to secede. He issued the Emancipation Proclamation in 1863 and made the total abolition of slavery the central promise of his re-election campaign in 1864.

Text issued by Lincoln in 1863 declaring free all slaves still held in Confederate territory. It applied neither to the slaveholding states that had stayed in the Union nor to Southern regions already occupied, which made an amendment to the Constitution necessary.

Amendment to the United States Constitution, ratified on December 6, 1865, that abolished slavery and involuntary servitude throughout the country. It contains one exception, punishment for a crime, which the Southern states exploited at once to force freed Black Americans back into unpaid labor.

A set of laws passed by the Southern states right after the Civil War to restrict the rights of freed Black Americans and turn them into offenders. They made it possible to sentence them to forced labor and send them back to the fields and plantations.

Living without a job or a permanent home, made a crime by the Southern states after 1865. Since most former slaves had neither work nor a roof, the law allowed them to be arrested in large numbers and sentenced to forced labor.

Amendment to the United States Constitution passed by Congress in 1866, guaranteeing every American equal protection under the law. It was meant to fight the Black Codes, but the Southern states kept finding loopholes to impose forced labor.

The name given to the racial segregation laws in force in the American South from the late 19th century to the mid-20th century. Under that regime, the laws that sentenced Black people to unfree labor survived for decades.

course_292_pourquoi_le_titanic_manquait_.explanation: British shipping company that owned the Titanic. Convinced that its liner was unsinkable, it refused to carry more lifeboats than the law required, to avoid spending more and setting a precedent for the rest of its fleet.

Engineer in charge of the Titanic's safety features. He designed davits able to hold four lifeboats each and first recommended 48 boats, before giving way to the company's pressure down to 20, while warning that it was not enough.

Crane-like metal arms fixed to a ship's deck, used to store lifeboats and lower them into the sea. Those Carlisle designed for the Titanic could each hold up to four boats, but the company never used that capacity to carry more lifeboats.

Advisory committee of the British government on merchant shipping matters. In May 1911 it reviewed the Titanic's safety features and approved 20 lifeboats, despite Carlisle's warning that the number was not enough.

Captain of the Titanic on her maiden voyage. Shortly after the collision with the iceberg, he had the lifeboats prepared knowing they would not be enough, and chose to present the evacuation as a simple precaution to avoid panic.

The International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea, created in the wake of the Titanic disaster. It imposed new safety rules on ships, including the obligation to carry enough lifeboats for everyone aboard.

course_293_pourquoi_l_angleterre_s_est_e.explanation: A drug made from the sap of the poppy, smoked in nineteenth-century China, which causes strong dependence and ruins the health of its users. Grown by the British in India, it was the smuggled product at the heart of the two wars told here.

Major port in southern China, today's Guangzhou, the only place where the Chinese empire allowed European merchants to trade before 1842. It was there that Lin Zexu took on the opium trade in 1839 and that a seizure triggered the second war in 1856.

Economic doctrine according to which goods should move between countries without customs duties or restrictions. The British invoked it to denounce China's trade rules and to justify opening its ports by force.
Region in the east of the Indian subcontinent, then under British rule. It was there that the British grew thousands of tons of opium every year to be smuggled into China.

Senior official of the Chinese empire sent to Canton in 1839 to stamp out the opium trade. The destruction of the British chests he ordered served as the pretext for the First Opium War; he is celebrated in China today as a hero of the fight against drugs.
Treaty signed in 1842 that ended the First Opium War. China opened five ports to British trade and ceded Hong Kong; it was the first of the "unequal treaties" imposed on China by foreign powers.

The name Chinese historians give to the period opened by the Opium Wars, marked by defeats, unequal treaties and interference by foreign powers. That memory still feeds China's distrust of any outside intervention.

course_294_pourquoi_l_irlande_affamee_ex.explanation: Catastrophe that struck Ireland from 1845 to 1852, when blight destroyed the potato crops on which poor farmers depended. It killed about a million people and drove as many as two million to emigrate, mostly to the United States and Britain.
Disease caused by a fungus-like organism that rots the leaves and tubers of the potato plant. It reached Ireland in 1845, destroyed up to half of the crop and set off the Great Famine.

Doctrine holding that the state should interfere as little as possible in the economy and let the market set prices and trade. In its name, the British government refused to halt exports of Irish food during the famine.
Historian specializing in the Great Irish Famine. She quantified the exports of grain, livestock and butter in 1846-1847 and argues that Britain, by letting them leave, indirectly caused the famine.

Historian of 19th-century Ireland. He answers Christine Kinealy by showing that Ireland imported more than three times as much grain as it exported during the famine, and that the exporting regions were not the worst hit.

Nineteenth-century Irish nationalist, author of the line "The Almighty sent the potato blight, but the English created the famine." His words sum up the reading of the famine as a British crime, still alive in Irish memory.

course_295_pourquoi_avons_nous_des_fusea.explanation: British railway company linking London to the west of England. In 1840 it was the first to set all its trains and stations to Greenwich time, a model soon copied by every railway in the country.

Time measured at the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, near London, and known as GMT. Adopted by British railways from 1840, it became in 1884 the universal reference from which time zones are calculated.

Bands of territory that share the same official time, offset from Greenwich time by a whole number of hours. Born in 1883 for the North American railroads, they spread across the world over the following decades.

American editor of railway guides in the 19th century. It was his division of the United States and Canada into five time zones that the railroad companies officially adopted in November 1883, in preference to rival proposals.

Meeting summoned to Washington in 1884 by American President Chester A. Arthur, with delegates from 25 countries. It made Greenwich time the universal time and set a 24-hour day beginning at midnight, without imposing time zones.

Scottish-Canadian engineer of the 19th century. At the Washington conference of 1884 he proposed dividing the globe into 24 zones of one hour each, every 15 degrees of longitude; the conference did not formally adopt his system.

The position of a place to the east or west, measured in degrees from a prime meridian, the Greenwich meridian since 1884. Because the Earth turns 360 degrees in 24 hours, 15 degrees of longitude correspond to one hour's difference.

course_296_l_ia_consomme_t_elle_beaucoup.explanation: Building that houses large numbers of computers whose job is to process and store the information behind online services. It is where every AI answer is produced, and where the electricity AI uses is concentrated.

Intergovernmental organization based in Paris that publishes reference analyses on energy around the world. Its reports supply the course's benchmarks: 1.5% of global electricity for data centers in 2025, 100,000 households for one AI-focused site.
Computer designed to handle data and run online services, stacked with others in the racks of a data center. Servers do most of the computing there and absorb about 60% of the electricity on average.

Phase in which an AI model is created, as computers work through enormous amounts of examples to learn patterns from them. It keeps very powerful machines busy for long stretches, but it does not repeat with every question asked.

Computation carried out by an already trained model to produce a response to a request. Unlike training, it happens again for every request, so a heavily used service keeps its computers busy all the time.
Unit measuring an amount of energy: what a one-watt device uses in one hour. The course's estimates are expressed in this unit, from 0.24 Wh to 3.91 Wh depending on the request.

Network of lines and equipment that carries power from generating plants to homes and businesses. Large AI data centers plug into it, and their clustering in certain areas sometimes forces local lines to be upgraded.

course_297_d_ou_vient_vraiment_l_electri.explanation: Network of wires and equipment linking the power plants and users of an area, from which almost every home draws its power. Several plants feed it at the same time, which is why no socket receives electricity from a single source.

Breakdown of the sources (coal, gas, nuclear, wind, solar, hydro) supplying a grid at a given moment or over a period. It describes what feeds the network, not a separate stream sent to each device, and it changes from hour to hour.
Bladed wheel spun by a moving fluid: steam, hot gases, water or wind. In a power plant it drives the generator; it is what coal, nuclear, gas, hydro and wind power have in common.
Machine that turns rotating movement into electricity, coupled to the turbine in a power plant's turbine hall. Only solar panels do without one, since they produce power directly from light.

Organization in charge of running the electricity grid and keeping generation and consumption in balance at every moment. It has power stations adjust their output and calls on batteries and other sources when the sun fades or the wind drops.

Energy sources that nature replenishes on its own, such as sunlight, wind and flowing water. In the United States they supplied about a quarter of large-plant electricity in 2025, a yearly average that hides large hour-to-hour swings.

Breakdown of the sources actually supplying the users of an area, imports included. It can differ from the mix produced locally, and it is what determines the carbon dioxide emissions linked to the electricity being consumed.

course_298_esope_a_t_il_vraiment_existe|.explanation: Legendary Greek fabulist, a slave according to tradition, said to have lived around 600 to 500 BC. Mentioned by Herodotus, Aristophanes and Plato, he may be no more than a name under which a very large number of anonymous fables were gathered.

Short invented story, often peopled with talking animals, that illustrates a truth or a moral. Born in antiquity, the form makes it possible to criticize the powerful without naming them, which explains its success among the weak.

Athenian statesman and philosopher of the 4th century BC. He is credited with the first known collection of Aesop's fables, put together long after the fabulist's supposed death, which makes the figure of Aesop even more uncertain.

Gaius Iulius Phaedrus, a Roman slave turned poet, who set Aesop's fables in Latin verse in the 1st or 2nd century AD. His collection fixed the popular image of Aesop: an ugly slave, born mute, then gifted with eloquent speech.

Egyptian goddess, protective mother and magician, whose worship spread throughout the Greek and Roman world. In the legend reported by Phaedrus, she is the one who gives speech to Aesop, who was born mute.
Twentieth-century British writer, author of Animal Farm (1945) and 1984. He took up the form of the fable, personified animals and a moral, to denounce the corruption of absolute power.

course_299_pourquoi_aurore_dupin_s_est_e.explanation: Assumed name under which an author publishes. In the 19th century it let a woman get around prejudice: Aurore Dupin signed George Sand, a man's name, without hiding for long that she was a woman.

French novelist, friend and lover of Aurore Dupin at the start of her career. Together they wrote Rose et Blanche (1831), signed J. Sand, and it is from his name that she drew her pseudonym, replacing the J with a G.

Famous French actress of the Romantic era and one of George Sand's best-known female lovers. The writer, bisexual but preferring the company of men, devoted an entire chapter of her autobiography to her.

French novelist, author of Madame Bovary and Sentimental Education. A great admirer and friend of George Sand, he addressed her in his letters as "Chère Maître," mixing the feminine and the masculine.

Polish composer and pianist settled in Paris, George Sand's companion for almost ten years. Their parting was bitter, and Sand drew on him for the weak and sickly character of Karol in Lucrezia Floriani (1846).

Popular uprising that governed Paris for a few weeks in the spring of 1871 before being crushed in blood. It was the last great political upheaval George Sand lived through, after the revolution of 1848.

Period from March to June 1815 when Napoleon, back from exile on Elba, regained power before his defeat at Waterloo. George Sand was eleven at the time: she grew up to the rhythm of these political shocks.

course_300_comment_le_journal_d_anne_fra.explanation: Hidden rooms at the back of the building housing Otto Frank's business at Prinsengracht 263 in Amsterdam, their entrance concealed behind a bookcase. The Franks, the Van Pels family and Fritz Pfeffer lived there in hiding from 1942 until their arrest in August 1944.

Anne Frank's father, a businessman in Amsterdam and the only survivor among the occupants of the Annex. After the war he received his daughter's notebooks, read them despite his grief and looked for a publisher: he is the one who brought the diary out in 1947.
A trusted employee of Otto Frank who brought supplies to the people hiding in the Annex. After the arrest, she picked up Anne's notebooks and kept them unread, hoping to return them to her one day.
Another of Otto Frank's employees who helped the people hiding in the Annex. She supplied the paper on which Anne rewrote her diary, then rescued the scattered pages with Miep Gies after the arrest.
Widow of the American president Franklin D. Roosevelt and a leading voice for human rights. Her introduction to the English-language editions of 1952 gave Anne Frank's diary a first-rank endorsement.

American novelist and journalist. His glowing review, when the American edition came out, contributed largely to the public success of Anne Frank's diary, after Otto Frank had struggled to find a publisher.
American award created in 1917 and given every year for journalism, literature and drama. The play The Diary of Anne Frank, which opened on Broadway in 1955, won it.

course_301_pourquoi_machiavel_a_t_il_ecr.explanation: Powerful family of bankers and patrons who dominated Florence from the 15th century onward. Their return to power in 1512 cost Machiavelli his post and, for a time, his freedom, before inspiring The Prince, written to win back their favor.

Florentine writer and diplomat (1469-1527), an official of the Republic of Florence until the Medici returned. Arrested, tortured and then exiled in 1513, he wrote The Prince to get a job back and became, despite himself, the founder of modern political thought.

Grandson of Lorenzo the Magnificent, ruler of Florence from 1513 and Duke of Urbino, who died in 1519. Machiavelli dedicated The Prince to him in the hope of a position; Lorenzo never offered him one.

A kind of treatise, common in the Middle Ages and the Renaissance, in which a scholar sets out for a ruler the qualities and conduct that make a good sovereign. The Prince borrows the form but replaces morality with effectiveness.

A way of doing politics based on the balance of power and real circumstances rather than on principles or ideology. The word is German and came much later, but the attitude it describes is already at the heart of The Prince.

A problem in political philosophy: can a leader, or must a leader, commit morally wrong acts for the good of the community? Machiavelli is one of the first to answer yes without hesitation, and the question is still debated today.

course_302_quel_est_le_plus_vieux_livre_.explanation: Region of the Near East between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, in modern-day Iraq, where the first cities and the first writing appeared. It is where the Epic of Gilgamesh was composed and then copied onto clay tablets for centuries.

One of the oldest and largest cities of Mesopotamia, famous for its walls. In the epic, it is the city Gilgamesh rules as a tyrant at the start, and to which he returns, calmer, at the end of his quest.
Wild man created by the mother goddess to humble Gilgamesh, who becomes his inseparable friend after a fight. His death, decreed by the gods, drives the king to set out in search of immortality.

Writing made of small wedge-shaped marks pressed into wet clay with a cut reed, invented in Mesopotamia. Its durability explains why two-thirds of the Epic of Gilgamesh have survived for four thousand years.
Ogre appointed by the gods to guard the Cedar Forest, a legendary place where kings went for timber. His death and the felling of the trees by Gilgamesh and Enkidu bring down the anger of the gods.
Mesopotamian goddess of love and war, whose lovers all come to a bad end. Spurned by Gilgamesh, she sends the Bull of Heaven against him, and its death leads the gods to condemn Enkidu.
The only man to have escaped death: a survivor of the flood with his wife, he was granted immortality by the gods. He advises Gilgamesh to give up his quest, yet still points him to a plant of youth.

course_303_pourquoi_certains_detestent_i.explanation: The scientific name for the sense of smell: the detection of odor molecules by receptors in the nasal cavity. It contributes as much as the tongue to the flavor of food, which is why a single smell gene is enough to change the taste of coriander.

Proteins carried by cells in the nasal cavity, each sensitive to certain molecules. They convert an odor into a nerve signal sent to the brain. A change in the gene that builds one of them alters the flavor perceived, as happens with coriander.

The gene that codes for the olfactory receptor sensitive to the aldehydes in coriander. A single-letter variant of this gene, found in 4 to 20% of humans depending on the region, makes the fresh herb taste like soap.

A family of odor molecules found in coriander leaves, responsible for their fresh, herby scent. Detected by the OR6A2 receptor, they are read as a soapy taste by people who carry the variant of the gene.

A variation of a single "letter" of DNA between two individuals, often shortened to SNP. This tiny change can alter how a gene works: in the case of OR6A2, it turns the flavor of coriander into a taste of soap.

course_304_pourquoi_rougit_on|Charles Da.explanation: British naturalist (1809-1882), author of the theory of evolution by natural selection. In *The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals* (1872), he studies blushing and describes it as the most peculiar and most human of all expressions.

course_304_pourquoi_rougit_on|sympatheti.explanation: The branch of the nervous system that prepares the body for action in the face of a threat: faster heartbeat, rising temperature, rush of blood. It is what dilates the vessels of the face and makes you blush, whether the alert comes from a blunder or a compliment.

course_304_pourquoi_rougit_on|fight-or-f.explanation: The emergency response triggered by the sympathetic nervous system when facing danger: the body gets ready either to defend itself or to run away. An embarrassing social situation is enough to set it off, and blushing is its visible trace.

course_304_pourquoi_rougit_on|social anx.explanation: A strong, lasting fear of situations in which one may be watched or judged by others. People who suffer from it often see themselves in a negative light, which amplifies the sympathetic response and makes them blush more easily.

course_304_pourquoi_rougit_on|exposure t.explanation: A psychological method that consists of facing feared situations gradually and repeatedly, until they no longer trigger fear. Applied to awkward social situations, it helps the brain stop treating them as a danger and reduces the fear of blushing.

course_304_pourquoi_rougit_on|mindfulnes.explanation: A practice that consists of paying attention to the present moment, sensations and emotions included, without judging them or trying to escape them. Faced with blushing, it teaches you to observe the rising heat without dreading it, which breaks the loop of fear.

course_305_pourquoi_deteste_t_on_entendr.explanation: Two folds of tissue in the larynx, at the top of the windpipe. Air driven out by the lungs makes them vibrate at high speed, which produces the sound of the voice, later shaped into words by the mouth and tongue.

The transmission of sound through the air: sound waves enter the ear canal, make the eardrum vibrate and then the small bones of the middle ear, before reaching the inner ear. It is the only channel through which you hear a recording of your own voice.

A spiral-shaped organ in the inner ear, lined with hair cells. It turns vibrations, whether they arrive through the air or through the bones of the skull, into electrical signals that the auditory nerve carries to the brain. It is where the two paths of your own voice meet.

Tiny hair-like structures standing on the surface of the cochlea's hair cells. They bend in time with sound vibrations and trigger the electrical signal sent to the brain. Without them, no vibration would ever become a perceived sound.

The transmission of sound through the bones of the skull, directly to the inner ear, bypassing the eardrum and the middle ear. When you speak, it adds to air conduction and enriches the voice you hear, something a recording cannot reproduce.

A notion from robotics and animation: an imitation of a human pleases us more the closer it gets, until, almost perfect but not quite, it provokes unease. A recorded voice, almost our own, may fall into it too.

course_306_pourquoi_rit_on_quand_on_nous.explanation: A light, "feathery" tickle, close to an itch, that can be felt almost anywhere on the body. It makes you shiver or scratch but does not trigger laughter: that is the job of the other kind, gargalesis.

A quick, firm tickle, confined to the armpits, neck, torso, stomach and feet, that produces wriggling and involuntary laughter. It is the kind the brain processes as play, and the kind you cannot inflict on yourself.

Sensory receptors in the skin that respond to mechanical, that is physical, stimulation: pressure, vibration, movement. They are the starting point of a tickle: their signal travels up to the brain, where it mixes with the emotional signals of play.

A messenger molecule of the brain, released in particular by the deep regions linked to reward and pleasure. Its release during tickling explains the positive association the brain builds with the sensation, despite the writhing it provokes.

A set of brain regions that pick out, among all the signals received, those that deserve attention and a response. Part of this network is active during tickling, alongside the areas that process humor and emotions.

A region of the brain's frontal lobe, folded over the insula, a deep area of the cortex. Together with the supplementary motor area, it is one of the two places where tickle laughter is set off, at a distance from the regions that process its pleasure.

An area of the frontal cortex involved in preparing and launching movements, especially sequences of movements. Together with the frontal operculum, it is where tickle laughter begins, which widens still further the brain circuitry engaged in this response.

course_307_comment_le_christianisme_est_.explanation: Roman emperor from 306 to 337, victor at the Milvian Bridge in 312 and the first emperor to support the Christians. He legalized their worship through the Edict of Milan, funded churches and convened the Council of Nicaea, without banning the old gods.

Decision taken in 313 by the emperors Constantine and Licinius: Christians may practice their faith freely and recover the property confiscated during the persecutions. Christianity became a lawful religion, but not yet the official religion of the empire.

Assembly of bishops convened by Constantine in 325 to settle the question of the nature of Jesus and his relationship to God the Father. It adopted the Nicene Creed, but did not end the quarrels among Christians.

Priest of Alexandria who taught that Jesus, created by the Father, was not his equal. His doctrine, Arianism, was condemned at Nicaea in 325, but it kept supporters, including among the emperors, for decades.

Name given by Christians to the traditional cults of the empire as a whole, with their many gods, their temples and their public rites. In the 4th century it remained very much alive in the cities, the countryside and the army, despite the rise of Christianity.

Emperor from 361 to 363, raised a Christian but won over to the old gods, hence his nickname "the Apostate," one who has renounced his faith. He tried to restore the traditional religion of Rome and cut off funding to Christian institutions.

Law of 380 signed by Theodosius I, Gratian and Valentinian II. It reserved the support of the state for the Christianity loyal to the Council of Nicaea and made it the official religion of the empire, far beyond the mere tolerance granted in 313.

course_308_quelle_a_ete_la_guerre_la_plu.explanation: Chinese scholar who failed the imperial examinations and, after reading Christian texts, proclaimed himself the younger brother of Jesus. He founded the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom, took the title of Heavenly King and died in 1864, shortly before the fall of Nanjing.

Competitive exams for recruiting the officials of the Chinese empire, based on the study of the Confucian classics. Passing them opened a prestigious career; Hong Xiuquan's repeated failures preceded his visions and the birth of the Taiping movement.

Tradition of thought inherited from Confucius, founded on respect for rites, hierarchy and family duties, which structured the Chinese state. Along with Daoism and Buddhism, it is one of the three great currents that the Taiping religion came to upset.
State proclaimed by Hong Xiuquan and his followers in southern China, with its own laws, administration and army. Based in Nanjing from 1853 to 1864, it collapsed when Qing troops retook the city.

The last imperial dynasty of China, in power from 1644 to 1912. It was against the Qing that the Taiping rose up, seeing in their rule the embodiment of an evil to be destroyed; the dynasty finally crushed the rebellion in 1864.

Major city of the Yangtze basin and former imperial capital, protected by massive walls. Taken by the Taiping in 1853 and renamed Tianjing, the "Heavenly Capital," it fell to the Qing in July 1864 after nearly two years of siege.
Fortified city on the Yangtze, upstream from Nanjing, held by the Taiping. Its extremely violent siege ended with its recapture by the Qing in 1861, which opened the road to the Heavenly Capital.

course_309_d_ou_vient_la_science_fiction.explanation: Greek writer of the 2nd century and a master of satire. His True Story, which sends its narrator to the Moon, is often described as a distant ancestor of science fiction, even though it works first of all as parody.

Period, above all in the 17th century, when observation, measurement and experiment transformed the European view of nature, with Galileo's telescope and Kepler's laws. It gave writers new material for imagining other worlds.

German astronomer (1571-1630) who established the laws of planetary motion. His Somnium, published in 1634 after his death, imagines a journey to the Moon and describes the Earth seen from space: science there becomes material for a story.

English novelist (1797-1851), author of Frankenstein, published in 1818. By telling the story of a scientist who creates life and loses control of it, she gave science fiction its modern shape, centered on responsibility and the consequences of technology.

Transformation of the economy and society by machines, factories and new technologies, starting in late 18th-century England. It feeds the anxiety of Frankenstein: technology changes life faster than its effects can be understood.

American editor of Luxembourg origin (1884-1967). He launched the magazine Amazing Stories in 1926, first spoke of "scientifiction," then established the term "science fiction" with Science Wonder Stories in 1929, giving the genre its name and its public.

course_310_qui_a_trace_les_frontieres_de.explanation: Meeting of the European powers held in Berlin from November 1884 to February 1885, at the invitation of the German chancellor Bismarck, to set the rules of colonial expansion in Africa. It did not draw today's borders, but it organized the competition between empires.

Principle adopted in Berlin: to have a territory recognized as its own, a state had to exercise real authority there, with administrators and armed forces. It pushed the European powers to turn their paper claims into actual conquests.

Area where one power is recognized by the others as holding privileged political and economic control, without necessarily administering it directly. The European empires divided Africa on their maps this way before governing it on the ground.

Powerful state in West Africa, in present-day Ghana, with Kumasi as its capital. It resisted the British for a long time, and they folded it into their colonial system only after several wars in the 19th century.

Latin phrase for the principle that a new state keeps the borders it held at the moment of independence. African states adopted it so that challenging every border would not degenerate into endless wars.

Organization founded in Addis Ababa in 1963 by the independent African states to defend their sovereignty and cooperation. From 1964, its leaders pledged to respect the borders inherited from colonial rule.

course_311_qui_a_invente_les_zombies|Vod.explanation: Religion of Haiti born from the meeting of West African beliefs, Catholic Christianity and the island's history, marked by slavery. It is in this world that the zonbi appears, a person deprived of their soul or their will.

course_311_qui_a_invente_les_zombies|bok.explanation: In Haitian tradition, a sorcerer who practices a secret magic and who can, it is said, seize a person's soul or will and turn them into a zonbi. He embodies the master who controls the creature, an idea taken up by the films of the 1930s.

course_311_qui_a_invente_les_zombies|Hai.explanation: Language born in Haiti in the time of slavery, formed from French and African languages, and spoken today by the whole population. It is in this language that the word is spelled zonbi, before becoming zombi in French and then zombie in English.

course_311_qui_a_invente_les_zombies|Ame.explanation: Period from 1915 to 1934 during which the United States occupied Haiti militarily and ran its administration. It brought American soldiers, journalists and writers to the island, and they took home stories of Vodou and zombies.

course_311_qui_a_invente_les_zombies|Wil.explanation: American journalist and writer, a great traveler drawn to cultures he found mysterious. His book The Magic Island, published in 1929, introduced Haitian zombies to the American public by presenting Haiti as a strange and dangerous place.

course_311_qui_a_invente_les_zombies|Geo.explanation: American director who made Night of the Living Dead in 1968, a black-and-white film that became a landmark of horror cinema. He invented the modern zombie: the dead rising and attacking the living with no master to command them.

course_57_l_invention_d_internet|Cold Wa.explanation: The indirect confrontation between the United States and the USSR from the late 1940s to 1991, without open war between the two superpowers. Fear of a Soviet attack led the American military to fund a communications network able to survive destruction: the future Internet.

course_57_l_invention_d_internet|Y2K bug.explanation: The fear, in the late 1990s, that computers storing the year as two digits would confuse 2000 with 1900 and trigger cascading failures. It shows how indispensable networked computing had already become by the turn of the millennium.

course_57_l_invention_d_internet|Paul Ba.explanation: American engineer who, in the early 1960s, experimented with packet switching to design a network able to withstand a Soviet attack. His work led directly to ARPANET, the ancestor of the Internet.

course_57_l_invention_d_internet|packet.explanation: A technique that cuts a message into small packets of data sent separately across the network, then reassembled on arrival. If one line is cut, the packets take another route: this is what makes the network resilient.

course_57_l_invention_d_internet|ARPANET.explanation: A computer network funded by the U.S. Department of Defense, whose first machines were linked in 1969. It put packet switching into practice and served as the model for the many networks that, joined together, would form the Internet.

course_57_l_invention_d_internet|router.explanation: A device that receives data packets and directs them to the next machine or network, all the way to their destination. Developed by British scientists, it is the part that allows ARPANET, and then the Internet, to move information around.

course_57_l_invention_d_internet|World W.explanation: A system launched at CERN in 1990 by Tim Berners-Lee that presents data from servers as pages linked by hyperlinks. It is not the same thing as the Internet: the Web is the layer that makes the network readable and navigable by everyone.
